Yet, the choice and assignment of colors to display elements can be challenging because colors have associations with a variety of meanings (e.g., blue on a map is associated with both water and cooler temperatures). In addition to making sure that the colors chosen for a display are discriminable from one another, the designer must make sure the concepts assigned to individual colors actually match the user’s semantic associations. In some instances, color choice is relatively easy, for example, when a designer needs to pick colors to represent the two major political parties in the U.S: Republicans are red and Democrats are blue. This is a strong association for most Americans. Color codes that are closely associated with the concept being represented (e.g., yellow for banana imports) do, in fact, result in faster graph interpretation than when color codes with low associations are used (e.g., lavender for banana imports) (Lin et al., 2013). But problems arise when colors have multiple associations, of which the color red is probably most problematic: red signals “danger” in most people’s mind. But this association is problematic when red is used to color code “Republican” or “China.”

It may be tempting to conclude that choosing colors (or other perceptual attributes) to represent concepts is relatively straightforward: Just ask users what colors they associate with concept X, Y, and Z. However, Schloss et al. (2018) have found that when users infer color meanings in an unfamiliar coding scheme, they do more than make “local assignment inferences.” Local inferences involve the user selecting the color with the strongest association with a concept, then proceeding to the next concept, eliminating the already-selected color from the option set. Instead, users make “global assignment inferences,” where they consider the total possible set of color-concept mappings and try to choose color meanings that maximize strong associations and minimize weak ones in the overall coding scheme.

As an example of this contrast between local and global assignments, imagine a new resident of a town who is trying to find the location of recycling sites by looking at a color-coded map. The town has three classes of recyclables:“yard waste,” “used electronics,” and “all other items (general recycling).” The locations of recycling centers for each type of refuse are indicated as black, blue, or green icons. Assuming that there is no accessible legend, or that the user fails to consult it, then how will the user infer color meanings? If using the local inference strategy, the user might see a green icon and select the strongest association that comes to mind, for example, seeing a green icon and associating it with “renewal” and hence “general recycling.” The remaining colors will be assigned in the same way. Use of the local inference strategy will result in slightly different color-meaning associations than when a global strategy is used. In the present case, assume the user’s association strength for all nine possible associations (3 colors X 3 meanings) are as follows:

| Association strength | Color-concept association |
| --- | --- |
| STRONG | Green - General Recycling Green - Yard Waste Blue - General Recycling |
| MODERATE | Black - Yard Waste Black - Electrical Items Blue - Electrical Items |
| WEAK | Green - Electrical Items Black - General Recycling Blue - Yard Waste |

If we assume the user is taking all (or most) of the possible associations into account, the coding scheme that both maximizes strong associations and minimizes weak ones is as follows: Blue: general recycling, green: yard waste, and black: electronics items. There is no possible solution where each of the associations are strong ones, but this solution eliminates the use of any weak associations. Note that this solution is different from the one that resulted from a local inference strategy, where green was assumed by the user to represent general recycling. Designers, like users, should consider the associations of all colors and concepts in their color coding scheme before deciding on the final color assignments. Fortunately for designers, there are now algorithms for assigning colors to display elements that are consistent with the way people appear to make inferences about color meanings (e.g., Lin et al., 2013).

Note that display elements other than color have associations that should also be heeded. Returning to our scatterplot showing the relationship between preferred room temperature and age, there are relatively strong associations between one of the variables and an important display element. Returning to our discussion in Section 4.5, the concept of temperature is associated with verticality, probably originating in the fixed orientation of early mercury thermometers (i.e., hot = high and cold = low). The displays in Figure 8 both make use of this association by plotting preferred temperature on the vertical axis. See Tversky (2001) for an extensive discussion of the use of space in mental and physical representations.

Domain knowledge is yet another important source of information brought by the user to display interpretation tasks.

Domain knowledge is knowledge about the actual topic or data sources that the designer attempts to portray (Flach, Bennett, et al., Chapter 36 in this volume). It includes the identity and description of agents, instruments, and actions that are part of a context or system, as well as of the sometimes complex interactions among these elements. Consider the knowledge needed to support the work of operators in dynamic, high-risk systems such as aviation, process control, and surgery. Representation aiding is a display design approach in the cognitive engineering tradition (Lee & Kirlik, 2013; Section 2) that has proven to be particularly valuable in these environments (Roth & Bisantz, 2013; Smith et al., 2006; Vicente & Rasmussen, 1992). The focus of this approach is on understanding the physical constraints of dynamic systems, a type of domain knowledge that may not be perfectly understood even by experienced operators. The goal is to match these constraints to the geometric properties of displays. Here, domain knowledge is not just a property of operators (display users), but also refers to the knowledge acquired by designers that is essential for the creation of specialized displays. The representation aiding approach pays particular attention to creating a representational architecture with configural properties, or emergent features, to aid operators as they solve both routine and unanticipated problems in pursuit of system goals (Bennett & Flach, 2013; Burns, 2013; Flach, Bennett, et al., Chapter 36 in this volume). Emergent features in displays can be helpful because they offload demands from operators’ limited-capacity working memory to more automatic perceptual processes. We will continue our discussion of emergent features as we consider principles of display layout below. Figure 9 provides an example of a display resulting from the representation aiding approach.

## 4.6.2 The User’s Goals

A general principle of display design is that no single display layout is likely to support all possible uses equally well. Thus, the organization of a display should be built upon a careful analysis of the task, or range of tasks, for which the display is likely to be used. It is sometimes helpful to think of displays as visual workspaces, similar in their need for organization to physical workspaces (e.g., the collection of tools on a workbench needed to assemble a product, or the EMS worker’s collection of medical instruments in an ambulance). Basic principles of workspace design dictate that frequently-used tools, or tools that are especially critical for completing important tasks, should be easy to find and retrieve. Our prior discussion of selective attention (Section 3) essentially described this principle as it relates to display design: High value information needs to be near the line of sight, should be easy to discriminate from surrounding information, and should attract attention. Another principle of workspace design is that tools that need to be used together to complete a step in the workflow, for example, a bolt and the wrench needed to manipulate it, should be placed close together. Display elements that need to be compared or mentally combined in order to complete a cognitive operation, should also be located close to one another.

The Proximity Compatibility Principle (PCP) is a general guide for the organization of display “workspaces.” In particular, it addresses how to match the structure of the workspace to the mental tasks of the user (Barnett & Wickens, 1988; Carswell & Wickens, 1987, 1996; Wickens & Andre, 1990; see Wickens & Carswell, 1995, for review). The PCP describes a number of design practices whereby display elements can be made to appear more proximal or visually related to one another; sometimes the PCP even advises that display elements be spatially conjoined. “High proximity” layouts are those that increase inter-element closeness or grouping. The question is: When should we use these high proximity layouts and when should we not? To answer this question, the PCP describes contingencies between mental operations and display layouts using the following two rules:

1. When two (or more) elements of a display must be integrated (e.g., compared, multiplied, subtracted) in the service of a single task—a feature we describe as “close (or high) mental proximity”—they should be placed in close physical proximity on the display.

2. When one element must be processed by itself, without distraction from other information sources (distant or low mental proximity requiring focused attention), its processing is best served when it appears more distant or distinct from its neighbors (low physical proximity).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 9 Rankine cycle display for monitoring the health of a nuclear power generating plant. The jagged line indicates the trajectory of the plant parameters (steam pressure and temperature) as they follow the constraints of the thermodynamic laws.

Hence there is a sort of “compatibility” between proximity in the mind (or the task) and proximity on the display. Of course, what this means is that no single display layout serves all tasks, for what may be best for integration tasks (“how does my speed compare with a maximum speed allowable?”) may not serve focused attention (“what is my current speed?”).

In order to put the general guidelines of the PCP into practice, we need to consider how specific design practices can lead to the impression of high or low display proximity. Fortunately, we have more than a century of research describing the lawful ways our perceptual systems parses raw sensory data into potential targets for attention, a process called perceptual organization (for reviews, see Peterson & Kimchi, 2013; Wagemans et al., 2012). Figure 10 shows several of the most important ways display proximity can be manipulated by a designer. Note, in Row (a), that changing the distance between elements is an important means of changing proximity, but it is hardly the only means. Items in a display can remain physically distant but be made to appear grouped together by making them look more similar (e.g., use a common color), connecting them with line segments, enclosing them in a common frame, or configuring them into parts of the same object.

To understand the costs that can be imposed by physical distance between items that must be integrated (high task proximity), consider the challenge of comparing a graph on one page of a textbook with a related graph on the back side of the same page. Would it not be better if the two graphs were side by side so that repeated page flipping would not be needed? Or consider the problem of using legends when interpreting line graphs. Many legends are presented in a “box” under or to the side of the graph itself, forcing the reader to scan between the graph lines and the legend to identify what each line represents. This scanning task becomes more challenging as the graph contains progressively more lines. It would be better if each graph line had its own label attached to it (Huestegge & Philipp, 2011). As a third example, consider the advantage of having an out-of-tolerance alarm light positioned next to the continuous display of the variable to which it pertains, rather than in a separate alarm-panel.

In these three examples, we can identify three costs of low proximity. There is a physical movement cost in the case of the textbook. There is a scanning cost in the case of the alarm panel and the graph. And in all three cases, there is increased cognitive load, as those moving or scanning between displays must do so while holding information in working memory from the first image (e.g., graph label) to the second (graph line).

Just as large physical distance (low display proximity) can cause costs in some situations, close proximity too can have a downside (see Row (b) of Figure 10). On the right, the oval indicator and the digital altitude reading are separated. It is easy to focus on one and ignore the other. On the left, they are overlaid. The very close physical proximity created by overlay can create clutter, making it hard to focus on one and ignore the other. Such overlay is often created when viewing the world beyond through a head-up or head-mounted display (Wickens, Ververs, & Fadden. 2004; Wickens, 2021; Stanney et al., Chapter 30 in this volume); such “high proximity clutter” may also be created by overlaying computer windows (Mori & Hayashi, 1995), or overlaying data-bases on a map (Kroft & Wickens, 2003; Wickens, 2020). Of course, the reader may ask, “Can’t we get the best of both worlds by placing the two displays adjacent, and not overlapping?” and the answer here is “Yes.” Adjacency will greatly reduce the costs of integration, but if there is at least 1∘ of visual angle separating an item from its neighbors, this will greatly reduce, and sometimes entirely eliminate, the costs to focusing attention. In some sense this 1∘ separation is the optimum trade-off of two cost functions.

Spatial proximity of information, despite its importance for facilitating integration, is not always available to the designer due to other layout constraints. In a map of the U.S. using the size of icons to indicate the prevalence of homelessness, the icons will fit in the boundaries of some states (i.e., large states with little homelessness) but would obscure surrounding states in other cases (i.e., small states with large homeless populations). Proximity can still be achieved by using linkages (e.g., lines) between the icon and the state it represents (Jolicoeur & Ingleton, 1991). Indeed, line graphs are formed by the addition of lines linking adjacent data points (Row (c) of Figure 10). Although the lines are not essential to understanding the trends, they still make those trends easier to visualize (Carswell & Wickens, 1996) creating an emergent feature as we describe below.

Another way to generate display proximity among items that cannot simply be moved closer is to exploit perceptual similarity, as shown in Row (d) of Figure 10. For example, two items to be compared may be highlighted in the same color (Wickens, Alexander, et al., 2004) or may both be flashed or oscillated in synchrony. This technique can be quite advantageous for an air traffic controller (ATC) who must consider the trajectories of two planes that are still far apart but on the same altitude and converging. On an ATC display cluttered with many other aircraft symbols, a highlighting tool (Remington et al., 2000) that can illuminate each aircraft of interest in a common color can greatly reduce the demands of such a comparison.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 10 Six examples of close (left side) vs. distant (right side) display proximity between information sources influencing different perceptual mechanisms.

The last design practice we will discuss for creating high proximity displays might be thought of as “extreme proximity” (see example in Row (e) of Figure 10). Object displays are created when two or more information sources (i.e., variables) are mapped onto different features of a single object. Line graphs are a simple and familiar object display, but there are many other examples differing in their level of abstraction and complexity. “Hat displays,” for example, are object displays that use the vertical position of the hat’s brim and crown to represent two variables and their difference (Witt, 2019). Another example is the “rectangle display, which uses height and width to represent individual values and produce other features that result from the combination of the two (i.e., area and overall shape) (Andre, Wickens, Moorman & Boschelli, 1990; Barnett & Wickens, 1988).

Some object displays, or glyphs, are used in large multiples superimposed on, for example, maps and vector fields, to represent multiple variables describing a single data point at each position (Ward, 2008). Common glyphs use attributes of a variety of objects to represent variables of interest, for example “arrows” (varying orientation, length, and shape of “arrowhead”), “stars” (varying the length of each ray), and “trees” (varying the length and orientation of branches). Note that color is often added to glyphs as an additional information-carrying property.

Glyphs and other object displays have the practical advantage of spatial economy, allowing more variables and data points to be presented in a single display while minimizing clutter. Consider weather maps, which provide data about multiple variables (e.g., temperature, wind speed, humidity, air pressure) at numerous locations. If we wanted to create a low proximity display of this information, we could create a separate map for each variable (e.g., a temperature map, a pressure map, etc.), but this design makes it difficult to integrate information about a single location to get an overall picture of the associated weather. We could increase display proximity by using a separate icon for each variable and then clustering them together near the location they describe, but this design quickly becomes cluttered. Finally, we could create a high proximity display that uses the features of a single glyph (e.g., attributes of an arrow) to represent the complete weather profile at each location, thus maximizing display proximity and minimizing clutter.

Spatial economy, although important, is not the only rationale for creating and using object displays. There is also evidence that perceptual organization constrains the deployment of attention, and that when we attend to a particular object we process its features more or less in parallel (e.g., Duncan, 1984; Egly, Driver & Rafal 1994; Egly, Rafal, Driver, & Starrveveld, 1994; Kimchi, Yeshurun, Spehar, & Pirkner, 2016).

The use of objects to represent multiple variables can, in the right circumstances, help us detect important data combinations, but may also make it difficult to decode information from any individual feature (Carswell & Wickens, 1996; Wickens & Carswell, 1995). Returning to our weather map with arrow glyphs (object displays), if a viewer wants to know whether the combination of weather conditions in Houston points to the approach of a tropical depression, then the all-or-none processing of the features in Houston’s glyph might be helpful in rapidly collecting and combining the available evidence. However, as we have seen elsewhere when using the PCP, design practices that create close display proximity can have negative consequences for low proximity focused attention tasks. Thus, if the user of our map is only interested in the wind speed in Houston, it could be difficult to isolate and categorize wind speed as, say, “good” if other weather features appear to be in ranges considered “bad.” That is, there could be conflict among the information provided by the various parts of the glyph.

Yet another advantage of object displays is that they sometimes present additional information—composite variables— that are simply not available if we look at the display’s component parts in isolation. We have referred to these “extra” information sources previously as emergent features (also see Bennett & Flach, 2013; Pomerantz & Pristach, 1989). To understand their benefits, take as an example a tree display, which consists of a trunk from which branches emerge. Individual variables are mapped onto the length and angle of each branch, for example they might represent security parameters for a communications network. There are a number of emergent features that result from the different configurations of the tree’s parts: symmetry, top-heaviness, overall “wilt.” The presence of these features, in and of themselves, is not sufficient to ensure the display will support the user’s performance. However, the emergent features may become beneficial if they appear (emerge) in circumstances that indicate important data relationships that are relevant to the user’s task, for example, serving as cues to important events or states (e.g., presence of a security breach).

Well-coordinated emergent features can be helpful because their detection reduces cognitive load by replacing the need for what would otherwise be a series of slow mental integrations. The importance of emergent features in the use of visual displays is revealed by the special phrases devised to describe them. For example, research scientists may describe the data in line graphs as “an inverted-U,” a “crossover interaction,” the “knee” and “elbow” of a plot, and “flattening the curve.” The following is a list of caveats regarding the application of emergent features in the development of high-proximity displays:

Emergent features are not restricted to object displays (Buttigieg & Sanderson, 1991; Pomerantz & Pristach, 1989; Seppelt & Lee, 2007). For example, the separate objects (i.e., separate bars) in Row (f) of Figure 10 can be organized to produce a useful emergent feature—collinearity of the bar tops, seen in the left version of the display but not in the right.

Feature similarity is important in the creation of emergent features. Consider why the emergent feature of collinearity is produced in the display on the left side of Row (f) but not on the right. The separate bars on the left have been grouped through their use of the same baseline. Another important ingredient in the formation of emergent features is use of the same physical dimensions to represent different variables across different objects. Thus, collinearity forms from variation of the height of multiple bars, but not from the designer’s variation of height on one bar, width on the next, orientation on the third, and so on.

Some types of object displays do not create emergent features. In general, object displays formed from geometric properties will produce emergent features but those that combine spatial and nonspatial dimensions (e.g., size and color) do not (Carswell & Wickens, 1996).

Emergent feaures should be mapped to important states or events of the represented domain. For example, the creation of the “collinearity” emergent feature in the left side of Row (f) is only useful if it signals task-critical information such as “all is normal” in an industrial process monitoring task.

Emergent features, like other display elements, must be consistent with a user’s semantic associations. This rule can sometimes be difficult to follow. The challenges associated with the use of the “face display” (which uses the features of a caricature face to represent different variables) is a cautionary tale. A recent application of faces (Lilford et al., 2014) used features such as mouth curvature and eyebrow orientation to represent personality characteristics of successful and unsuccessful sales representatives. Unexpected relationships among the component variables (represented as facial features) may lead to unintended and unfortunate emergent features (facial expressions). We are particularly attuned to human faces, and viewers may become disoriented if an expression (e.g., looking menacing or confused) does not fit their associations with successful members of a sales force.

Once again, the main implication of the PCP for designers is to direct them toward certain display design practices (i.e., creating proximity of displayed elements) that will reduce effort in information integration tasks. It directs designers toward other practices (i.e., isolating and segregating elements) in situations when focused attention is required. These overarching guidelines, however, are not the only consideration during display design. The designer must still consider likely users knowledge, as well as sensory properties of display elements related to detectability and discriminability (see Proctor and Proctor (Chapter 3 in this volume).

## 4.6.3 The Designer’s Goals

Until now, we have assumed that the goals of the designer and user are aligned. The designer’s goal is to create an information artifact that supports the user’s goals. However, there are times when the goals of the designer are distinct from those of the user, for example, in displays used for persuasion. The design of quantitative displays for policy papers, advertisements, financial reports, campaign websites, scientific reports, and newscasts are all often structured to communicate predetermined messages in order to influence the viewer.

There are a number of strategies that designers can use to create displays that persuade, all of which leverage what we know about cognitive processing. Some of the strategies deal simply with making the information the designer wants to communicate easier to find, interpret, and recall. However, some strategies can lead to displays that mislead or deceive (a goal that may be intended in some forms of advertising, political persuasion or even propaganda). Our purpose here is not to encourage the use of information processing principles in the service of deception, but to make it easier for display users to detect such deceptive designs.

We can make graphs and visualizations more persuasive by using one or more of the following principles:

1. Draw the viewer’s attention, via salience, to data that supports the designer’s argument (and away from those that do not).

2. Make relationships among data values that support the target argument easy to detect and recall.

3. Make relations among variables that support the target argument look more impressive than they actually are (i.e., than when accurately quantified).

4. Make it difficult for the viewer to make inferences that are not consistent with the target argument.

Our understanding of perceptual organization and selective attention can inform application of the first two principles. Our understanding of perceptual illusions (see Section 4.3) and display expectancies (i.e., viewers’ knowledge about particular formats) can inform the latter two principles.

The problem of misleading graphs has been addressed in a number of reviews (Kosslyn, 2006; Szafir, 2018). Accounting and finance researchers have identified instances of misleading graphs in financial reports and have documented the frequency of some deceptive practices (e.g., Beattle & Jones, 2000; Frownfelter-Lohrke & Fulkerson, 2001). Recall that emergent features are important cues to the significance or implications of a graphed data set. One familiar example is the slope of the line in a line graph. An upward slope in financial reports is associated with “good performance,” for example, representing increasing profits across time. However, there are many examples of financial graphs designed to give the impression of a steep upward slope when, in fact, the real increase is modest (Frownfelter-Lohrke & Fulkerson, 2001). The designer can make the slope appear steeper simply by compressing the horizontal axis scale, or by expanding the vertical axis scale. It is possible to either increase or decrease the perceived urgency of an exponential growth curve, for example of a pandemic, by expanding or compressing, respectively, the scale of the vertical axis depicting number of cases. When research participants are asked to use graphs with compressed horizontal axes to make financial decisions, they act as though they are mainly responding to the (unreliable) slope of the line. Thus, the designers were successful in making their financial report appear more positive, and participants made decisions that were more favorable to the company whose data was graphed (Arunachalm, Pei, & Steinbart, 2002; Pennington & Tuttle, 2009).

An even more troubling practice involves the labeling of years along the horizontal axis of a line graph in order to make a downward trend (i.e., bad performance) look positive. Graphing conventions for time series data usually show time increasing from left to right (Tversky, 2001). The expectancies of viewers can be exploited by simply reversing the order of years causing the direction of an apparent trend to reverse (Figure 8). Once again, research participants seem to depend on the direction of the slope, without reference to the axis labels, when using the graphs to make decisions (Arunachalm et al., 2002). Instead, users have just employed their format expectancies or graph schema discussed in Section 4.6.1. The failure of readers to check the association of years and data points is not surprising. As we have seen, scanning to integrate information can lead to increased effort. The combination of strong expectancies for the layout of this format, along with a focus on detecting trends rather than reading specific data points, may easily make most of us miss this graphical sleight of hand.

In order to make this sort of manipulation more difficult to carry out, we could of course require standardized formats in financial documents, just as these are encouraged, although not mandated, by scientific journal guidelines (Gillan, Wickens, Hollands, & Carswell, 1998). Such deceptions could also be made less likely by requiring increased visual proximity between data points and the horizontal axis. Proximity could be increased in a number of ways, for example by the use of light grid lines or by replacing the “points” along the line graph with year labels. Interpretation errors made with misleading graphs are often compounded when viewers must later recall the same information (Pennington & Tuttle, 2009; Tversky, 1991).

The viewer of a graph can sometimes infer the goals of the designer by observing how elements are organized on a graph. Specifically, which elements did the designer connect perceptually using the display proximity practices we have described in this section? Why are some data points grouped together spatially, or connected by similar color or physical linkages, and other data points are not? This sort of “reverse engineering” can tell us what the designer thinks is important about the data, which may or may not be consistent with our own beliefs or interests.

In conclusion, forming effective multi-element displays can sometimes be as much a creative “art” as it is a science. However, principles based on information processing research can provide guidance. On the one hand, display design should take into consideration both the knowledge of likely users and their tasks/goals. Display interpretation, on the other hand, should incorporate inferences by the user about the goals of the designer. We now turn to the types of complex, cognitive tasks that often require well-designed visuospatial displays, for example, to support situation awareness, navigation, and problem solving.

## 5 COMPREHENSION AND COGNITION

In Section 4, we described the operator’s perceptual tasks as, in many ways, invoking decision-making, problem-solving, or reasoning processes. Detection involves decisions about criterion setting. Identification often involves estimations of stimulus probabilities. Size and distance judgments in 3D space involve the formulation of perceptual hypotheses. For the most part, however, these higher-level cognitive processes occur rapidly and automatically, and outside our awareness. In this sense, perceptual reasoning is a far cry from the effortful, deliberate, and often time-consuming process that we are very aware of when trying to troubleshoot a malfunctioning computer, find our way through an unfamiliar airport, understand income tax forms, or choose among several medical treatments. Before discussing such higher-order cognitive tasks in this section, we describe the critical limits of working memory. As we will see, the parameters of working memory constrain, sometimes severely, the strategies we can deploy to understand and make choices in many types of tasks.

## 5.1 Working Memory

Working memory refers to the limited number of ideas, sounds, locations, images, or events that we can mentally maintain and manipulate at any point in time. There is a long tradition in memory research of distinguishing between a large-capacity, durable memory system, our long-term memory, and a more transient, limited, and vulnerable memory system of the sort we discuss here (see Baddeley, 2012; Cowan, 2017, for reviews). Both memory systems are involved in all complex cognitive tasks, but the limits of one may be more apparent than those of the other in any particular case. For instance, when we log into a website by entering an often-used security code, our ability to complete the task will largely depend on the efficiency with which we can retrieve the code from long-term memory. Alternatively, when we try to transcribe a randomly-generated, temporary security code from one mobile device to another, our performance will depend more heavily on working memory. Further, if the temporary security code is long and contains few familiar patterns, or if we are interrupted in the middle of the transcription task, we will probably exceed our working memory capacity and we may have to begin the task again, after some suitable grumbling.

Across many types of memory tasks and information domains, there appear to be two fundamental ways that our working memory system limits performance (Oberauer et al., 2018). First, our recall accuracy and recognition speed decline as the number of independent items to be held in memory increases. Second, the longer we must keep information active in working memory, the more likely we are to lose some or all of it, particularly if we are faced with additional information or competing task demands during the retention period. Although only a small set of items can be held in working memory, and only briefly at that, there are a number of factors that make it easier for us to cope with working memory’s limits (Oberauer et al., 2018). Some of these moderating factors, described below, can be exploited by designers to keep working memory demands manageable for operators.

Most designers want to know exactly how much (or little) information we can hold in working memory. The traditional answer comes from George Miller’s classic 1956 article, and he provides his estimate in the title, “The magical number seven plus or minus two.” The memory span, the number of stimuli most people can accurately recall immediately after presentation, ranges from five to nine independent items. The qualifier “independent” is critical, however, because physically separate items that are stored together as a unit in long-term memory may exist in working memory as a single entity—a chunk. For English speakers, the letter string “H–T–E” contains three items to remember, whereas the rearranged string “T–H–E” contains only one.

Although Miller’s estimate is still cited, subsequent research revealed that our memory span is almost certainly more limited; and his lower bound (7 − 2 = 5), closer to reality in tasks beyond the laboratory. If we are prevented from using memory strategies, such as rehearsal and rearrangement of items into familiar chunks, most of us have spans in the three- to five-chunk range (Cowan, 2010). If a delay is introduced between information presentation and recall, and if we make the realistic assumption that this interval is filled with sounds, new objects, events, and messages (i.e., life goes on), the span rapidly shrinks (Brown, 1959; Peterson & Peterson, 1959). For example, memory decay can occur in less than 20 seconds for verbally delivered navigation information (Loftus et al., 1979) as well as for visuospatial radar information (Moray, 1986). In situations with high cognitive load, such as during difficult steps in laparoscopic surgery, brief delays to answer questions can lead to critical errors such as missed steps (Feuerbacher et al., 2012). Loss of activation of short-term goals (i.e., “What was I doing?”) has been associated with tragic consequences (Reason, 1990).

The multi-component model of working memory (Baddeley, 2012; Baddeley & Hitch, 1974) describes working memory as having four essential parts. First, there are two units that store different types of information—the phonological loop and the visuospatial sketchpad, described more fully below. Information from these storage units is managed by a central executive which also incorporates information from long-term memory to create rich representations of objects that combines information from auditory, visual, and other domains. These representations are held temporarily in an episodic buffer. Although the episodic buffer is newer to the multi-component model than the other memory stores (Baddeley, 2000), it is important for situation awareness and comprehension, which we turn to in the next two sections of this chapter. The contents of the episodic buffer are also central to our experience of consciousness.

Most research on working memory has probed the limits of the phonological loop, so named because it is associated with our silent repetition of words, letters, and numbers. The phonological loop stores a limited number of sounds for a short period of time. The number of words that can be held in working memory, therefore, is related to the number of syllables they contain; we can hold fewer multi-syllable words than single-syllable words (Bhatarah, Ward, Smith, & Hayes, 2009). The contents of the phonological loop are disrupted by many of the same conditions that make it difficult to hear and understand spoken content, for example, when there is ongoing irrelevant speech (e.g., Salame & Baddeley, 1982), concurrent tones (e.g., Jones & Macken, 1993), or instrumental music (e.g., Schlittmeier et al., 2012). Sounds that are easily confused when spoken are also more likely to result in recall errors (Farrell & Lewandowsky, 2003). for example, we are more likely to recall “U-Z-J-L” in the correct order than we are to recall “T-D-P-B.” Finally, the contents of the phonological loop can be lost when we generate internal speech that competes with the items we are to recall. Research on performance anxiety provides a practical example of how two internally-generated phonological streams can compete with one another. In this research Coy et al. (2011) manipulated the performance anxiety associated with memory “tests” by altering the instructions given to different participants. Those who received the more anxiety-inducing, judgmental instructions performed more poorly on a verbal working memory task, but only when their anxiety was associated with verbal rumination during task completion.

In addition to the phonological loop, Baddeley and Hitch (1974) proposed a visuospatial sketchpad that stores information about the appearance and location of objects. The need for two storage units, each serving a different information domain, arose from evidence that combined visuospatial and verbal memory sets could be remembered better than combined verbal sets or combined visuospatial ones (e.g., Repovš & Baddeley, 2006). Relying on similar reasoning, the visuospatial sketchpad was itself subdivided into two stores—one specialized for storing visual features such as color and shape and another specialized for storing information about movement and location (Logie, 1995). There appeared to be low levels of interference between visual and spatial information (Klauer & Zhao, 2004).

Just as the presence of auditory noise interferes with retention of information in the phonological loop, the presence of “visual noise” interferes with recall of visual attributes (i.e., it reduces the vividness of visual images) (Baddeley & Andrade, 2000). For recall of spatial rather than visual information, such as memory for a series of matrix locations, tones varying in location selectively disrupt performance; the tones do not disrupt memory for other visual attributes (Smyth & Scholey, 1994). Memory for spatial locations is also disrupted by eye movements during the retention interval (Postle et al., 2006). Interference from scanning is consistent with suggestions that people keep spatial information active in the visuospatial sketchpad by repeatedly generating “scanning plans” of the locations they want to remember (Awh, Jonides, & Reuter-Lorenz, 1998). Finally, as was the case with the phonological loop, anxiety can interfere with the contents of the visuospatial sketchpad. However, it is anxiety associated with fear of harm (i.e., anticipation of a shock) rather than performance anxiety that disrupts recall of spatial information. Degree of physiological arousal is correlated with poorer performance in a spatial working memory task but not in a verbal one (Shackman et al., 2006).

The multi-component model’s third storage unit, the episodic buffer, was added by Baddeley (2000) to account for our ability to recall recent events, real or imagined, involving objects composed of attributes bound together from multiple domains (e.g., visual, spatial, verbal, tactile, etc.). This buffer also incorporates knowledge from long-term memory to create a meaningful tableau. Limits in the contents of the episodic buffer depend on the processing efficiency of the central executive, which selects, integrates, rehearses, and manipulates information from all storage units. Each individual’s personal working memory capacity reflects the central executive. Working memory capacity is correlated with performance in complex cognitive tasks such as reading and reasoning, and is also related to measures of intelligence (Conway et al., 2003). A prominent view of these individual differences (Engle, 2002) contends the differences do not simply arise from variation in the size of memory storage units, but rather they result from differences in the functioning of the central executive. In particular, they reflect the central executive’s role in suppressing both external and internal information that can create conflicts with an individual’s immediate goals. This view has informed recent attempts to develop working memory training programs, the value of which is still a matter of debate (Au et al., 2015; Melby-Lervag, Redick, & Hulme, 2016).

## 5.1.1 Working Memory, Learning, and Training

Two, or sometimes three of the components of working memory are active when material is to be learned—in skill training or more formal academic classroom instructions: maintenance rehearsal of words just heard (the phonological loop) or graphics just seen (the scratchpad) and the central executive, necessary to link the rehearsed material to that in long term memory and form deeper associations with the new material (i.e., to learn). It is important to consider the properties of working memory in order to maximize the efficiency of this process. For example:

Irrelevant verbal sounds can disrupt the phonological loop, and loading too much into the phonological loop (the lecturer talks too fast) can compete with operations of the central executive to store the material in LTM. (This provides an advantage for learning from text.)

In the context of the proximity compatibility principle, discussed in Section 4.6, spatial proximity or contiguity between text and graphics, and temporal contiguity between speech and pictures or graphics will both minimize the loss of information in the phonological loop before the graphic images are viewed.

Feedback regarding performance, a vital element in learning should be presented immediately after performance, so memory of the characteristics of that performance, and how it was generated will not have been degraded, when it is compared with the feedback (e.g., what the learner should have done).

## 5.1.2 Implications for Design

For the designer, it is important to recognize the constraints imposed on our performance by working memory, and to realize that design interventions can help reduce memory load, reduce recall errors, and minimize the performance costs for those with lower working memory capacities. The working memory construct, as we have seen above, can contribute to the design of instructional materials and methods. Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) has been influential in its use of research on working memory to guide instructional design (Paas et al., 2003, 2010; Sweller, 1994, 2011). However, it is possible to extend working memory principles to fields as diverse as environmental design, personnel selection, public safety, and consumer product design. Below we provide some very general design guidelines that can be broadly applied:

1. Whenever possible, avoid exceeding the 3–5 chunk capacity of working memory. This capacity limit will determine, for example, the number of variables we can process when understanding statistical interactions (Halford, Baker, McCredden, & Bain, 2005) as well as the number of basic ideas that can be presented as bullet points on a presentation slide (Durso, Pop, Burnett, & Stearman,. 2011).

2. Encourage chunking of larger memory sets. Breaking a string of digits into groups of 3–4 items may help people identify patterns and reduce the apparent number of physical items to a smaller number of mental units (Wickelgren, 1964); “354-6773” is easier to recall than “3546773.” This is, of course, what the social security number does.

3. Information for different tasks should be split across different storage units. For example, the phonological loop could be used for one task while the visuospatial sketchpad could be used for a second. Exclusively using either store for both tasks might easily exceed working memory capacity. More will be said about this intervention when we discuss multi-task performance in Section 7.

4. For information to be stored in the phonological loop, designers should select items that are easy to pronounce. In general, fewer syllables are better than more. Consider the following shopping list: “green onions, aubergine, dried plums.” This list should be rejected in favor of the following synonymous list: “scallions, eggplant, prunes.” The second list will be easier to rehearse while trying to find a smartphone on which to record it.

5. Minimize the time information must be held in working memory before it can be used. For example, voice menu systems should always allow users to select a desired menu options as soon as they encounter it rather than forcing them to wait until all the menu options have been read. Longer delays also increase the possibility of interruptions when using many systems, for example when having to actively dismiss a popup notification while entering financial information into a spreadsheet.

6. Avoid visual scanning while information is being held in the visuospatial sketchpad. Thus, a first responder who has found the likely location of a victim in cluttered, unfamiliar, and distorted terrain should not have to scan long lists of information to find appropriate communication codes. Scanning is known to disrupt maintenance of sketchpad information. In this context, one key aspect of the proximity compatibility principle discussed in the previous section, is to avoid requiring information search while a piece of information must be retained in working memory.

7. Avoid irrelevant sounds in tasks that make intensive use of the phonological loop. Put colloquially, make sure people can “hear themselves think” (Banbury et al., 2001). Consider a scientist who is comparing research results in two journal articles. Remembering the numeric information from one while reading comparable information in the other will be disrupted by nearby conversations, background music, and the sound of a motorcycle leaving a nearby parking lot. This principle leads to one of the strongest arguments against open, multi-person office plans.

8. Minimize the similarity of to-be-remembered items. Errors in recall are more likely when to-be-remembered information is similar in meaning, sound, form, or location. Thus, an air traffic controller might have particular difficulties remembering a series of aircraft with similar call signs (UAL 235, UAL 325). Where possible, mitigation of this cost can be achieved by reducing totally redundant items that compete for working memory capacity; for example, in the above, using terms UA 235, UA 325 instead.

9. Consider variations in the capacity of working memory among operators. These variations seem to be associated with differences in the fluency of the central executive and, hence, with success in many complex cognitive tasks (Engle, 2002). These findings have implication for staffing decisions and selecting operators in memory-intensive jobs. Variation in working memory capacity should also be explicitly considered in the design requirements for products targeted at heterogeneous populations.

10. In any cognitive task analysis, ensure that working memory demands are explicitly called out (e.g., delay between encoding and use, and capacity required), and efforts are made to mitigate these in design.

11. Working memory is heavily involved in text comprehension as we will see in Section 5.3, but it is also critical in speech comprehension of training and educational materials (i.e., materials that must be committed to long-term memory). Here the speaker should consider the working memory load of the attentive listener/learner, when she must simultaneously listen (occupying the phonological loop) and process to transfer to long-term memory (a central executive function). Both require limited resources (see Section 7) and hence can compete with each other. This process is hindered when the speaker talks too fast, rapidly saturating the phonological loop. For the instructor or speaker, the overload is mitigated by imposing short silent pauses just after the delivery of critical information. These considerations are closely associated with the cognitive load theory of instruction (Paas, van Gog, & Sweller, 2010) and are covered above and in more detail in Section 5.3.

## 5.2 Dynamic Working Memory, Keeping Track, and Situation Awareness

Much of the research devoted to working memory has examined tasks in which information is delivered in discrete batches and the goal is to remember as much of the information as possible. However, there are many other tasks in which the operator must deal with continuous information updates with information continuously encoded, stored, and then “dumped.” Moray (1981) studied several running memory tasks that simulated the demands of a more continuous input stream, and he found the typical memory span to be well less than five chunks. In some cases, it was difficult for subjects to keep track of items more than two places back in the queue. Yntema (1963) demonstrated that the way information is organized has a direct impact on supervisors’ abilities to keep track of values of multiple attributes of several objects (e.g., status and descriptions of several aircraft). Supervisors had greater success keeping track of a few objects that varied on many different (and discriminable) attributes than in keeping track of variation in a few attributes for many objects. In the former case there are fewer opportunities for confusion than in the latter case, and confusion is a major source of disruption in working memory (Hess Detweiler, 1995).

This earlier research on running memory anticipates the rapid growth of interest over the last three decades in situation awareness (SA) or, colloquially, our understanding and use of information about “what’s happening” during dynamic tasks (Banbury & Treselian, 2004; Durso et al., 2007; Endsley, 1995, 2015; Endsley in Chapter 17 in this volume, Endsley & Garland, 2000; Tenney & Pew, 2006; Wickens, 2008). Endsley (1995) provides a more formal definition of SA, one that has been adopted by many current researchers: SA is “the perception of the elements of the environment within a volume of time and space, the comprehension of their meaning, and the projection of their status in the near future.” This definition suggests that SA has three stages or “levels”: (1) perception or “noticing”; (2) understanding or comprehending, and (3) projecting or prediction. These three levels of situation awareness can be tied directly to different aspects of information processing and, therefore, failures at different levels will require different types of training or design interventions.

Stage 1 SA, perception or noticing, traces directly to issues of selective attention and attentional capture, discussed in Section 3. Indeed, Jones and Endsley (1996) found that a majority of aircraft accidents attributable to loss of SA were related to breakdowns at this first stage. Likewise, Durso et al. (2007) found failures of stage 1 SA to be responsible for many SA-related problems encountered in air traffic control. This is not surprising given our previous discussion of how easily we can fail to notice significant changes in dynamic systems (e.g., the “change blindness” phenomenon; see Section 3.3). In general, failures of stage 1 SA typically indicate the need for interventions involving display design, especially the use of alerts and attentional cueing. However, because sampling of information in dynamic environments also involves long-term memory in the form of knowledge about “where and when to look. training interventions may also be considered (e.g., Hoffman et al., 1998).

Stage 2 SA, understanding the implications of events noticed in stage 1, depends heavily on the limits of working memory as they apply to keeping track of evolving situations (e.g., the pilot asks: “Where was that traffic aircraft the last time that I looked?”). The episodic buffer of working memory proposed by Baddeley (2003), with its connections to long-term memory, may be necessary to explain the ability of skilled performers to hold more information for longer periods than would be expected on the basis of the decay rates established for other working memory stores. Likewise, Ericsson and Kintsch (1995) have used the concept of long-term working memory with its automatic activation of relevant knowledge structures in long-term memory to explain the unusual ability of experts to maintain and integrate relatively large amounts of information across time. For operators who may lack extensive experience, and even for experienced operators who may be interrupted by other tasks, displays of system history may also be helpful in understanding the implications of current events in light of prior observations (St. John et al., 2005; St. John & Smallman, 2008).

The stage 3 component, prediction and projection, is perhaps the most complex and may depend to a greater extent than the other two stages on the expertise and training of the operator. Accurate prediction of an evolving situation certainly depends on current perception and understanding (stages 1 and 2), but it also requires a well-calibrated mental model of the dynamic process under supervision (Gentner & Stevens, 1983; Wilson & Rutherford, 1989), a mental model that can be “played” in response to the current data, in order to predict the future state. For example, an air traffic controller with a good mental model of aircraft flight characteristics can examine the display of the current state and turn the rate of an aircraft and project when (and whether) that aircraft will intersect a desired approach course, thereby attaining a satisfactory separation. A well-calibrated mental model resides in long-term memory, but to play the model with the current data requires perception of those data as well as the active cognitive operations carried out in working memory. In some cases, prediction can be approximated by using an expert-acquired script of the way a typical situation unfolds. However, unless active processing (stage 1) of incoming perceptual information is carried out, there is a danger that projection will be based totally on expectancies of typical situations and that unusual or atypical events will be overlooked. Naturally, stage 3 SA can benefit greatly from accurate predictive displays (Wickens et al., 2000, Yin et al., 2015).

It should be noted, finally, that situation awareness is a construct that is resident within the perceptual–cognitive operations of the brain. It is not itself a part of the action stage (other than the actions chosen to acquire new information to update SA; Wickens, 2015b).

## 5.3 Text Processing and Language Comprehension

Comprehension of language calls on many of the same cognitive operations used to maintain situation awareness (Durso et al., 2007, Endsley, Chapter 17 in this volume). Just as operators of dynamic systems must recognize objects in a constantly changing environment, readers must identify linguistic elements in an ongoing string of symbols. Just as operators depend on their knowledge of the work domain to relate objects to one another to form coherent scenes, readers depend on their knowledge of word meanings and syntax to turn words into coherent ideas. And just as operators create and update a mental model of “what’s happening” by integrating scenes into event streams, readers create and update a mental model of ideas and events in order to “get the gist” of textual material. Although we will focus on written language in this section, the principles and processes we describe can often be extended to other types of language output, for example, speech and signing.

Functionally, in human factors, comprehension can serve two different purposes. Immediate comprehension, as in interpreting a warning label, following assembly instructions, or enjoying a book, involves interpreting the meaning of words for the current activities (e.g., successful compliance, assembly, or entertainment respectively). In contrast, learning involves comprehension of verbal material that is required to be stored in long term memory, to be reused some minutes, hours or days in the future. In human factors, learning is typically accomplished through training, to be discussed in detail in Chapter 16 in this volume by Salas et al. Naturally there is often considerable overlap between these two purposes. Just as you may be enjoying a good book in the moment, so too, a chapter later, you may want to recall aspects of a particular character you encountered an hour earlier. And as you follow assembly instructions for one device, you would like to rely on memory of that assembly if you have to follow those same instructions for another device. Text comprehension is necessary for both purposes, and the means by which comprehension is achieved is described below.

Text comprehension processes can be roughly divided into three neurobiologically-plausible subsystems: memory, unification, and control (i.e., Hagoort’s 2013 MUC model). First, the memory subsystem organizes perceptual primitives into identifiable units (e.g., words) by retrieving linguistic and semantic knowledge from long-term memory. The unification subsystem integrates word-level information from the memory subsystem into more complex mental representations, such as propositions, topic structures, and situation models. The cognitive resources demanded by the unification subsystem necessitate a control subsystem that selects, inhibits, stores, retrieves, and manipulates information to meet a reader’s goals. We introduced concepts relevant to the control subsystem when we discussed working memory, especially the role of the central executive (Section 5.1). Our focus here will, therefore, be the unification subsystem, including the corpus of knowledge it requires and the operations it performs.

## 5.3.1 The Knowledge Base for Comprehension

There are many guidelines available to help those creating text-based products—from legal documents and drug labels to college textbooks and assembly instructions. Authors are routinely advised to use vocabulary appropriate for the intended readers. This guideline, though important, reflects only one type of knowledge required for comprehension—the reader’s lexicon, or “mental dictionary.” Reading also requires knowledge of orthography (i.e., the rules that map visual marks to sounds and words), syntax, literary devices (i.e., expectancies about the function and structure of different text genres), as well as general world knowledge (Perfetti & Stafura, 2014).

World knowledge and knowledge of literary devices are important, as we will see, when comprehension depends on making inferences about information not explicitly stated in the text. Consider the following sentences from a news story: “A member of the school’s maintenance staff reported that she mopped the floor. She also said she could not find a ‘slip hazard’ warning sign.” To make sense of the second sentence, we need to know that mopping makes a floor wet and that wet floors are often slippery. In addition, our familiarity with the genre of “news story” will lead us to expect that it will report a negative event. As a result, most of us will assume that the above sentences were taken from a story about someone who was injured after a fall on the newly-mopped floor. We will say more about the way such inferences are made below. The main implication of world knowledge for inference generation, however, is that authors must (1) be aware of the inferences readers must make to understand the text, and (2) determine whether the intended readers are likely to possess the knowledge required to make the inferences.

Comprehension problems can arise not only when readers have insufficient knowledge about a particular domain, but also when they fail to retrieve relevant knowledge when it is needed (McKoon & Ratcliff, 1992). To address this problem, text designers will sometimes use strategically-placed cues to prime relevant knowledge. In a classic study, Bransford and Johnson (1972) had participants read a series of instructions about washing clothes. Readers given instructions preceded by the descriptive title, “Washing Clothes,” had much better comprehension and recall of the instructions than readers who received untitled instructions. The title activated whatever knowledge readers already had about washing clothes, and they could then use that knowledge to more easily interpret the written instructions. We caution that titles can also prime knowledge in ways that lead to misunderstanding and can even contribute to disinformation. For example, Ecker et al. (2014) found that what readers remembered from a news story, and the inferences they made about it, depend on whether the title headline emphasized the article’s main topic or a secondary issue.

Readers’ experience with different types of written materials—different genres, literary conventions, and standardized formats—can influence their reading goals, strategies, and ultimately what they understand and recall. For example, readers who believed that a text was a literary story recalled more surface detail and less situational detail than readers who believed the same story was a news article (Zwaan, 1994). Even short training sessions that cover the content and organization of specific types of texts can have positive effects on comprehension. For example, explicitly teaching patients with low medical literacy the main parts to expect on drug labels results in better understanding of information critical for safe drug use (Tai, Bae, LaRue, & Law, 2016).

Finally, the use of knowledge-appropriate vocabulary has both direct and indirect effects on comprehension. When terms tagged as difficult in journal articles and electronic health records were manually replaced with simpler terms—a process called lexical simplification—readers’ comprehension indeed improved (Kandula, Curtis, & Zeng-Treitler, 2010). Automatic lexical simplification, based on the assumption that a word’s frequency of use is a proxy for word familiarity, has resulted in text that is perceived as simpler by readers (Leroy, Kauchak, & Mouradi, 2013). Reader perception is important because of its potential influence on a reader’s engagement with the material.

## 5.3.2 Text Unification Processes

Lexical simplification alone may be insufficient in many cases to increase the comprehensibility of a document. Sentence simplification that depends on limiting sentence length may also be an insufficient intervention. Yet, many familiar readability metrics rely exclusively on such easily-measured features as word and sentences length to estimate text difficulty (e.g., the Flesch-Kincaid “reading grade” score generated by word processing applications). Text difficulty also depends on text factors that directly affect the reader’s ability to integrate words and sentences to extract more complex conceptual representations (Crossley et al., 2008). One such characteristic is a document’s text coherence. Coherence reflects the number and type of links among important ideas in a document; it is an estimate of how easy it will be for readers to detect key relationships. Leroy and colleagues (2013) found that enhancing coherence led to a 15% gain in comprehension of text that had already been lexically simplified.

Text unification is the weaving together of ideas from text with one another and with world knowledge to build two types of mental representations: (1) a propositional textbase; and (2) a situation model (Kintsch & Rawson, 2005). To form the propositional textbase, readers parse sentences into propositions, which are elemental ideas that represent a state or event. For example, the instruction, “Connect the USB cable to the wall charger,” includes propositions that describe (1) the type of cable (USB); (2) the type of charger (wall); and the event that relates the cable and charger (connect). The propositional textbase is a network of such propositions. Each new proposition the reader encounters is added to the network, assuming the reader identifies a relationship between each new idea and earlier ones. The situation model, in turn, is an elaboration of the textbase that incorporates the reader’s domain knowledge and may result from the translation of textbase information into new mental codes, for example mental images or mental maps. When we read the instruction “Plug the USB cable into the wall charger,” we may create an image of a USB cable already connected to a wall charger which, in turn, is plugged into an electrical outlet. Note that the outlet is not directly mentioned in the instruction. Nevertheless, based on our experience with wall chargers, we will probably infer that we will need to find an outlet to use. We might also incorporate into our situation model information about room layout, showing the location of the nearest outlet.

The operations that create the textbase and situation model can put heavy demands on working memory (see Section 5.1). The reader engages in an ongoing cycle linking newly formed propositions with older ones. To be integrated into the textbase, propositions must be in working memory together (Kintsch & Rawson, 2005). However, working memory only holds approximately four propositions (Kintsch & Van Dijk, 1978). If propositions are the units that compete for access to working memory stores, it follows that the difficulty of a sentence is more closely related to its propositional density than its word count. The importance of working memory constraints on reading comprehension is also supported by extensive research on individual differences in working memory capacity. Over a wide variety of reading tasks, those readers with lower working memory capacities comprehend text more poorly than other readers (Peng et al., 2018).

As a general rule, any text (or task) features that increase demand on working memory are a threat to reading efficiency and comprehension. Recall that information in working memory, if not constantly rehearsed, is quickly lost. The longer ideas must remain active in working memory while a person is reading, the more likely they will be unavailable when needed to support the incorporation of incoming information into the reader’s evolving text base. Interruptions—by on-screen pop-ups, auditory alerts, haptic reminders, phone calls, text messages, and pure mind wandering, to name a few—are a nearly ubiquitous source of reading delays (see Section 7.1). Foroughi et al. (2016) found that even brief disruptions in reading were detrimental to recognition and comprehension measures. However, interruptions were mainly a problem for those with smaller working memory capacities. Note that pauses during reading can result from factors other than ones external to the task. Even the need to scroll down a webpage to continue reading can lead to comprehension loss, again harming comprehension of readers with low working memory capacities more than others (Sanchez & Wiley, 2009). Features of hypertext reading, such as added decision times and navigation delays compared to linear text, may also impose demands on working memory that disrupt comprehension processes (DeStefano & LeFevre, 2007).

A fundamental process during text unification, noted earlier, is the generation of inferences. Readers, often without being aware, “fill in” information not explicitly available in the text in order to add coherence to their textbase and further elaborate their situation models. Sometimes inferences are drawn with little effort; in other cases, inference generation is more akin to problem solving. In either case, the need to draw inferences can lead to comprehension errors. In some cases, inference generation can be time-consuming. Consider the following statement that greeted a voter as s/he entered his or her security code into an electronic voting machine (from Redish, 2005): “THE BALLOT HAS BEEN ACTIVATED.” The voter may reasonably wonder about the implications of the statement. Assuming the voter has a limited knowledge of electronic voting, s/he might have the following questions (left) and may infer a variety of possible answers (right).

| Questions | Potential inferences |
| --- | --- |
| Which ballot are “they” talking about? | 1. The last voter’s2. Mine |
| Why did the ballot become activated? | 1. The last voter submitted his/her ballot.2. I entered my code.3. I did something wrong. |
| What happens now? | 1. The last voter’s vote gets tallied.2. I can start filling out my ballot.3. I’ve lost my chance to vote. |

In this case, the correct inferences would be that (1) the ballot in question is his or hers, s/he activated it by entering his or her code, and that s/he can start filling it out. Of these, the most important inference is surely the last. To minimize the time and effort the voter put into this cascade of inferences, and to avoid misunderstanding, the message should be rewritten: “YOU MAY NOW FILL IN YOUR BALLOT.” Note that the original example uses the passive case and the better example uses the active case. An active case is often easier to understand.

It may be tempting for authors and designers to try to avoid the need for readers to make any inferences at all, but this is difficult and often impossible. Generating some kinds of inferences may even be advantageous for skilled readers. Compare the following sentences: “To vote for your preferred candidate, find the oval by his or her name and fill it in.” “To vote for your preferred candidate, find the oval by your preferred candidate’s name and fill the oval in.”

The second sentence avoids the need to infer relations between pronouns and prior referents. Yet, there is evidence that simple pronoun assignment is resolved automatically, and most readers will find the first sentence easier to read (Gordon & Chan, 1995).

How the text designer will resolve the tradeoffs between having longer, more explicit text and shorter ones that requires more inferences will depend on the cost of misunderstanding. However, when inferences are necessary, the designer should focus on factors that affect the likelihood that readers will make the correct inferences easily. We have already considered a central design rule for improving inference generation by readers: Make sure that readers have the right knowledge available at the right moment. Recall that this may mean cueing information from their long-term memory, perhaps by analogies to material known to be familiar, or making sure that information is still activated in working memory. Designers should also be aware that some types of inferences are simply more difficult for readers to make. For example, readers are more likely to infer causal antecedents than they are to infer causal consequences (Magliano et al., 1993). This means that our hypothetical voter is more likely to generate ideas about why his or her ballot is “activated” rather than to anticipate the consequences of ballot activation. The relative difficulty of generating consequence inferences is one justification for favoring active directives (e.g., “you may now vote”) over passive status descriptions (e.g., “the ballot has been activated”).

## 5.3.3 Use of Negatives

Negatives such as “not” or “no” should be used with caution when designing instructions. There are two primary reasons for this. First, when read or heard rapidly or under poor visibility or with background noise, the negative may not be perceived at all and the positive meaning of the phrase is inferred as the default. This can sometimes have serious consequences as when the negative is missed in the phrase “Do not turn on the power until after XXX is done”. When such negatives are included in instructions, they should be made quite salient: “Do NOT . . . .”. Second, negatives add cognitive complexity to understanding, particularly when they are compounded to create double or triple negatives (Clark & Chase, 1972), as we sometimes see in legal documents or court opinions. A double negative can often be expressed as a single positive, reducing the cognitive load on the listener or reader.

## 5.3.4 Nonverbal Cues in Documents

In the previous section, we have mainly used the term “text” to refer to linear strings of markings—lines forming letters, letters forming words, words forming sentences. Other visual attributes, such as use of space, contrast, and color, are also important for conveying information about a document’s meaning and structure. Collectively, these features are called text signals, and they support deeper comprehension in a variety of ways (Lemarié, Lorch, Eyrolle, & Virbel, 2008). The use of italics helps direct the reader’s attention to important ideas. Headings of different sizes and degrees of indentation can give the reader a preview of topic structure. Word color on a website can identify the availability of supplemental information via hyperlinks. Space between text segments can indicate a shift in time or place in a story. To demonstrate the impact of text signals, many studies have documented the detrimental effects of stripping them from text (Lorch, 1989). Imagine how your reading of this chapter might change if there were no indentations, no italicized terms, and if headings were buried between sentences in a text string. In fact, this is the problem faced by users of text-to-speech systems, for example the screen readers that support those with dyslexia and visual impairments (Lorch et al. 2012; see Chapter 47 in this volume by Vanderheiden et al.). There are ongoing efforts to translate visual text signals into auditory ones; however, current translations often compromise text comprehension by interrupting the flow of words (e.g., when the word “link” is spoken before every hyperlinked phrase on a web page).

Although we have focused on the processing of verbalpropositional content in this section, we have seen that language processing also involves visuospatial thinking. Spatial patterns that are part of text layout can contribute to the model we form of topic structure. Visual imagery may be incorporated into our situation models. We next describe, in more depth, our capacity for spatial orientation and spatial thinking.

## 5.4 Spatial Awareness and Navigation

Language comprehension sometimes taxes working memory, particularly the phonological rehearsal loop and central executive. However, people may often use text to generate representations of spatial relations. This spatial facet of text and language comprehension has been particularly prominent in recent discussion of the “situation models” that we develop when reading or listening to a story (e.g., knowing where in a room all the characters are sitting). We now turn to a task that relies more heavily, for many people, on the capacity limits of the visuospatial sketchpad (Logie, 1995) or, more generally, spatial working memory and spatial cognition (Shah & Iyiri, 2005)—navigating through our worlds, both real (finding our way through a maze of looping suburban streets and cul-de-sacs; Taylor et al., 2008) and virtual (searching a complex computer-displayed multi-dimensional database; Wickens et al., 2005; Whitlock, Smart, & Szafir, 2020).

## 5.4.1 Geographical Knowledge and Learning

Thorndyke (1980) has studied the knowledge that people use when finding their way about. Of particular interest is Thorndyke’s claim that increased familiarity with an area causes changes not just in the amount of detail contained in our mental representation of that area stored in long-term memory, but in addition, the actual type of mental representation (analog versus verbal/symbolic), as well as its frame of reference, may evolve in a predictable way. After an initial encounter with a city, neighborhood, or building, we may develop landmark knowledge. If told that his or her destination is beside the “telephone tower,” a person with landmark knowledge will scan the environment visually until spotting something that appears to be the tower and will then strike off in its direction. Thus, the newcomer has the knowledge necessary to recognize the landmark but has no knowledge about its location. For the person with landmark knowledge alone, wayfinding would be impossible if the landmarks were obscured. This problem has become commonplace as once-salient landmarks have become obscured by new and often taller structures. The problem for urban planners, then, is to ensure that landmarks (both natural and designed) remain easily visible and distinctive in order to serve their navigational function for years to come.

With more experience traveling about an area, we typically develop an ordered series of steps that will get us from one location to another. These sets of directions, called route knowledge, tend to be verbal in nature, stated as a series of left–right turns (e.g., “Go left on Woodland until you get to the fire station. Then take a left … ”), often punctuated by landmarks.
