Navigation along these routes may be rapid and very automatic; however, limited knowledge of the higher-order relations among different routes and landmarks still limits navigational decision making, making it difficult, for example, to figure out shortcuts and particularly difficult to recover when lost (Newcombe, 2018). With still more extensive wayfinding experience, or with specific map study, survey knowledge may be acquired. Survey knowledge is an integrated representation of the various routes and landmarks that preserves their spatial distance relations.

It allows people to point in the direction of unseen landmarks and recover when off-route. This analog representation is often referred to as a cognitive map.

The type of representation—route versus survey—that best supports performance in various wayfinding tasks, like so many other aspects of mental (and display) representation, depends on the nature of the task or problem. Thorndyke and Hayes-Roth (1982) compared route training (actual practice navigating between specific points in a large building) to survey training (study of the building map). Route training appeared to facilitate people’s estimates of route distance and orientation, while survey training appeared to facilitate judgments of absolute (Euclidean) distance and object localization. Differences in cognitive abilities as well as training are associated with superior survey knowledge (Newcombe, 2018).

## 5.4.2 Navigational Aids

Although we can often navigate through environments on the basis of our acquired knowledge stored in long-term memory, whether route, survey, or even landmark, there are many other circumstances in which we require displayed navigational aids which are perceived. These aids may take on a wide variety of forms, ranging in the degree to which guidance to a target is supported: from tightly guided flight directors in aircraft and turn signs on highways to route lists to electronic maps (in-vehicle displays based on GPS; Schwering et al., 2017) that highlight one’s current position, to simple paper maps. Furthermore, electronic maps can vary in the extent to which they rotate so that the direction of travel is “up” on the map, and both electronic and paper maps can vary in terms of whether they present the world in planar or 3D perspective view as the latter is seen in many in-vehicle navigation displays (see Section 4.4).

To understand which kinds of maps support the best spatial information processing to accomplish navigation, it is important to briefly consider the information processing stages involved in this process. The navigator must engage in some form of visual search of both the navigational aid (to locate the final destination, intermediate goals, and current location) and the environment or a displayed representation thereof (to locate landmarks that establish the current location and orientation). The navigator must then establish the extent to which both are congruent, determining the extent to which “where I am” (located and oriented) agrees with the intermediate goal of “where I want to be.” Finally, the traveler must choose an action (e.g., turn right) to move from the current location toward the goal. Establishing this congruence as well as choosing the action may require any number of different cognitive transformations that add both time and effort to the navigational task (Aretz, 1991; Gugerty & Brooks, 2001; Hickox & Wickens, 1999; Wickens et al., 2005, 2010).

An example of two of these transformations is represented in Figure 11, which represents the information processing of a pilot flying south through an environment depicted on a north-up contour map. To establish navigational congruence, the pilot must rotate the map mentally to a track-up orientation and then envision the contour representation of the 3D terrain to determine its congruence with the forward view. Both of these information transformations are effortful and time-consuming and provide sources for error. In particular, those sources involved with mental rotation of maps have been well documented (Aretz, 1991; Eley, 1988; Gugerty & Brooks, 2001; Macedo et al., 1998; Olmos, Liang, & Wickens, 1997; Warren, Rossano, & Wear, 1990).

Different transformations may be required when other navigational aids than the 2D map are provided. For example, verbal descriptions of landmarks (“the big church”) will also require some transformations to evaluate against their visible 3D spatial counterparts. Transformations may also be required to “zoom in” to a large-scale map (Kosslyn, 1987) in order to establish its congruence with a close-in view of a small part of the environment. Modeled in terms of processing operations such as visual search and spatial transformations, one can then determine the form of navigational aids that would be of benefit for certain tasks. For example, electronic maps are beneficial if they highlight the navigator’s current location, thus obviating visual search of the map. Highlighting landmarks on the map, which are salient in the visual world, will also reduce search.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 11 Mental rotation required to compare the image seen in an ego-referenced forward field of view (top) with a world-referenced north-up map (below) when the aircraft is heading south. The map image is mentally rotated (right) to bring it into lateral congruence with the forward field of view. It is then envisioned in three dimensions to compare with the forward field of view.

Rotating maps in a track-up orientation will help navigation by eliminating mental rotation (Aretz, 1991; Olmos et al., 1997; Wickens, 1999), and if shown in 3D perspective, give a realistic picture of what a landmark looks like. Presenting guidance information in a 3D format (Section 4.4), like one would see looking ahead into the environment itself, will also reduce the magnitude of any sort of transformations and considerably improve navigational performance (Wickens & Prevett, 1995; Wickens et al., 2005). The benefits of a 3D view will be enhanced if the viewpoint of the display corresponds to the same zoom-in viewpoint as that occupied by the navigator, looking forward, rather than a viewpoint that is behind and from the outside (Prinzel & Wickens, 2008–2009: Wickens & Prevett, 1995). These viewpoint relationships, as manifest in an aircraft navigation display, are shown in Figure 12, which depicts the viewpoint location (top row) and the view seen by a pilot (bottom row) in an immersed or egocentric view (a and b). (These two views differ in terms of their geometric field of view.) Panel (c) represents an external or exocentric view. Panel (d) represents a 2D coplanar view, which was discussed in Section 4.4.

Expressing navigational guidance in terms of command route lists (e.g., “turn left at X; go three blocks until Y”) will also eliminate the need for many of the spatial cognitive transformations that may be imposed when spatial maps are used, since the language of command is thereby expressed directly in the language of action. Such congruence can account for the benefits of route lists over spatial maps in many ground navigation tasks (Streeter et al., 1985). A second advantage to such route lists is that they can be presented auditorlly and represented phonetically in working memory mentally in a phonetic or verbal code, thus reducing competition for the spatial processing resources that are involved in many aspects of environmental scanning and vehicle navigation (Section 7). The verbal descriptions inherent in route lists are well suited for some navigational environments, particularly human-designed environments (cities) with objects that are easily labeled, have distinct unambiguous landmarks, and can easily be discriminated by counting (the “fourth house”). In many naturalistic environments, however, where features are defined by continuous, not categorical, properties and may be confusable, route lists are more problematic and should be coupled with redundant spatial or pictorial guidance.

The most direct levels of navigational guidance that eliminate most or all levels of mental transformations (e.g., a flight director, the 3D forward-looking display shown in Figure 12a, or a verbal route list) will provide for effective navigation while en route. However, such displays may do a disservice to the navigator who suddenly finds himself lost, disoriented, or required to make a spontaneous departure from the planned route (Ishikawa & Takahashi 2014; Reiner et al., 2020; Schwering et al., 2017). Also, those features that make a navigational display best for guidance will harm its effectiveness to support the spatial situation awareness (Section 5.2) that is necessary for a successful recovery from a state of geographical disorientation (Wickens, 1999; Wickens & Prevett, 1995). This is an important trade-off between the immersed 3D view of Figure 12a, which is good for guidance, but because of its “keyhole view” of the world, it is poor for maintaining global situation awareness, a task better supported by the exocentric view of Figure 12c.

The transformation in (a) is minimal; in (b) and (c), modest; and in (d), large. Views (a) and (b), however, reduce more global situation awareness.

Finally, we note that the immersed 3D view makes a poor tool for route planning, an activity that we turn to in the following section. Interesting innovative navigational display concepts are described for worlds that are both real (Schwering et al., 2017) and virtual (Reiner et al., 2020). Further analysis of the relationship between navigational task and the optimum navigational display can be found in Wickens, Vincow, & Yeh (2005) and Wickens, Hollands, et al. (2013).

## 5.5 Planning and Problem Solving

Our previous discussion has focused on cognitive activities that were heavily and directly driven by information in the environment (e.g., text, maps, or material to be retained in working memory). In contrast, the information-processing tasks of planning and problem solving are tied much less directly to perceptual processing and are more critically dependent on the interplay between information available in (and retrieved from) long-term memory and information-processing transformations carried out in working memory.

## 5.5.1 Planning

The key to successful operation in many endeavors is to develop a good plan of action (Miller, Galanter, & Pribram, 1960). When such a plan is formulated, steps toward the goal can be taken smoothly without extensive pauses between subgoals. Furthermore, developing contingency plans will allow selection of alternative courses of actions should primary plans fail. As an example, pilots are habitually reminded to have contingency flight plans available should the planned route to a destination become unavailable because of bad weather.

Planning can typically depend on either of two types of cognitive operations (or a blend of the two). Planners may depend on scripts (Schank & Abelson, 1977) of typical sequences of operations that they have stored in long-term memory on the basis of past experience. In essence, one’s plan is either identical to or involves some minor variation on the sequence of operations that one has carried out many times previously. Alternatively, planning may involve a greater degree of guesswork, and some level of mental simulation of the intended future activities (Klein & Crandall, 1995; see Chapter 37 in this volume). For example, in planning how to attack a particular problem, one might play a series of “what-if” games, imagining the consequences of action, based again on some degree of past experience. Hence a surgeon, in planning how to manage a potential future operation, might mentally simulate the future body conditions and reactions of the patient under different proposed surgical procedures to see if the intended actions might compromise patient safety.

Consideration of human performance issues and some amount of experimental data reveals four characteristics of planning activities. First, they place fairly heavy demands on working memory, particularly as plans become less script based and more simulation based. Hence, planning is a task that is vulnerable to competing demands from other tasks. Under high-workload conditions, planning is often the first task to be dropped, and operators become less proactive and more reactive (Hart & Wickens, 1990). The absence of planning is often a source of poor decision making (Orasanu, 1993; Orasanu & Fischer, 1997). Second, perhaps because of the high-working-memory demands of planning, in many complex settings, people’s planning horizon tends to be fairly short, working no more than one or two subgoals into the future (Tulga & Sheridan, 1980). To some extent, however, this characteristic may be considered as a reasonably adaptive one in an uncertain world, since many of the contingency plans for a long planning time horizon in the future would never need to be carried out and hence are probably not worth the workload cost of their formulation. Furthermore, the longer the planning horizon in an uncertain world, the greater is the likelihood that things may change and long-range plans must be abandoned or substantially modified.

Third, given the dependency of script-based planning on long-term memory, many aspects of planning may be biased by the availability heuristic (Schwarz & Vaughan, 2002; Tversky & Kahneman, 1974), discussed in more detail in Chapter 6 in this volume. That is, one’s plans may be biased in favor of trajectories that have been tried with success in the past and therefore are easily recalled.

Fourth, researchers in decision science have observed what is known as the planning fallacy or planning bias whereby planners consistently underestimate the time it will take them to complete a plan, as if overconfident that their own skills will be fluently engaged, or underestimating the probability that an unforeseen delay will be encountered (Buehler et al., 1994; Kahneman, 2011; Weiss, Buehler, & Griffin, 2016).

A final human factors and cognitive issue is that effective planning depends upon effective prediction of the future. Here research also reveals one limitation and two important biases in spatial prediction: (1) on maps, such as an air traffic control display, people are better at extrapolating an angle, than a position along a trajectory based on its velocity (Herdener et al., 2016); (2) the rate of exponential growth or acceleration, like that of a pandemic in its early stages tends to be underestimated, as if we make a linear extrapolation from the final observed data points, rather than follow the accelerating curve (Waganaar & Sagaria, 1975); and (3) people tend to underestimate the variability of predicted trends and predicted probabilities (Wickens et al., 2020) with the implications that they fail to prepare adequately for extremes, in particular “worse case” scenarios.

Consideration of such vulnerabilities leads inescapably to the conclusion that human planning is a cognitive informationprocessing activity that can benefit from automated assistance, and indeed, such planning aids have been well received in the past for activities such as flight route planning (Layton et al., 1994), ship navigation (Lee & Sanquist, 2000; Sidoti et al., 2017), and industrial scheduling (Sanderson, 1989). Such automated planners provide assistance that need not necessarily replace the cognitive processes of the human operator but merely provide redundant assistance to those processes in allowing the operator to keep track of plausible courses of future action.

## 5.5.2 Problem Solving, Diagnosis, and Troubleshooting

The three cognitive activities of problem solving, diagnosis, and troubleshooting all have similar connotations, although there are some distinctions between them. All have in common the characteristic that there is a goal to be obtained by the human operator; that actions, information, or knowledge necessary to achieve that goal is currently missing; and that some physical action or mental operation must be taken to seek these entities (Levine, 1988; Mayer, 1983). To the extent that these actions are not easy or not entirely self-evident, the processes are more demanding.

Like planning, the actual cognitive processes underlying the diagnostic troubleshooting activities can involve some mixture of two extreme approaches. On the one hand, situations can sometimes be diagnosed (or solutions to a problem reached) by a direct match between the features of the problem observed and patterns experienced previously and stored in long-term memory. Such a pattern-matching technique, analogous to the role of scripts in planning, can be carried out rapidly, with little cognitive activity, and is often highly accurate (Rasmussen, 1981). This is a pattern of behavior often seen in the study of naturalistic decision making (Kahneman & Klein, 2009; Zsambok & Klein, 1997; see Lehto, Chapter 6 in this volume).

At the other extreme, when solving complex and novel problems that one has never experienced before, a series of diagnostic tests must often be performed, their outcomes considered, and based on these outcomes, new tests or actions taken, until the existing state of the world is identified (diagnosis) or the problem is solved. Such an iterative procedure is typical in medical diagnosis (Caryon et al., see Chapter 53 in this volume). The updating of belief in the state of the world, on the basis of the test outcomes, may or may not approach prescriptions offered by guidelines for optimal information integration, such as Bayes’s theorem (McCarley & Benjamin, 2013; Yates, 1990; see Chapter 6 in this volume by Lehto and Nanda).

In between these two extremes are hybrid approaches that depend to varying degrees on information already stored in long-term memory on the basis of experience. For example, the sequence of administering tests (and the procedures for doing so) may be well learned in long-term memory even if the outcome of such tests is unpredictable and must be retained or aggregated in working memory. Furthermore, the sequence and procedures may be supported by (and therefore directly perceived from) external checklists, relieving cognitive demands still further. The tests themselves might be physical tests, such as the blood tests carried out by medical personnel, or they may involve the same mental simulation of what-if scenarios that was described in the context of planning (Klein, Orasanu, Calderwood, & Zsambok, 1993).

As with issues of planning, so also with diagnosis and problem solving (see Lehto and Nanda, Chapter 6 in this volume), there are three characteristics of human cognition that affect the efficiency and accuracy of such processes. First, as these processes become more involved with mental simulation and less with more automatic pattern matching, their cognitive resource demands grow and their vulnerability to interference from other competing tasks increases in a corresponding fashion (see Section 7). Second, as we noted, past experience, reflected in the contents of long-term memory, can often provide a benefit for rapid and accurate diagnosis or problem solutions. But at the same time, such experience can occasionally be hazardous, by trapping the troubleshooter to consider only the most available hypotheses: often those that have been experienced recently or frequently and hence are well represented in long-term memory (Schwarz & Vaughn, 2002; Tversky & Kahneman, 1974; see Lehto and Nanda, Chapter 6 in this volume). In problem solving, this dependence on familiar solutions in long-term memory has sometimes been described as functional fixedness (Adamson, 1952; Levine, 1988).

Third, the diagnostic/troubleshooting process is often thwarted by a phenomenon referred to alternatively by such terms as confirmation bias and cognitive tunneling (Levine, 1988; Nickerson, 1998; Wickens, Hollands, et al., 2013; Woods et al., 1994; see also Lehto and Nanda, Chapter 6 in this volume). These terms describe a state in which the troubleshooter tentatively formulates one hypothesis of the true state of affairs (or the best way to solve a problem) and then continues excessively on that track even when it is no longer warranted. This may be done by actively seeking only evidence to confirm that the hypothesis chosen is correct (the confirmation bias) or simply by ignoring competing and plausible hypotheses (cognitive tunneling).

Collectively, then, the joint cognitive processes of planning and problem solving (or troubleshooting), depending as they do on the interplay between working memory and long-term memory, reflect both the strengths and the weaknesses of human information processing. The output of each process is typically a decision: to undertake a particular course of action, to follow a plan, to choose a treatment based on the diagnosis, or to formulate a solution to the problem. The cognitive processes involved in such decision making are discussed extensively in Chapter 6, as are some of the important biases and heuristics in diagnosis discussed more briefly above.

## 5.5.3 Creativity

Creativity is formally defined as the production of effective novelty (Cropley, 1999). To be creative, it is not enough for us to generate scores of new ideas; we must also evaluate these ideas and identify those that satisfy specific goals (e.g., to be entertaining, appealing, safe, or effective). Finke et al. (1992) argue that creativity involves the same cognitive processes and mental representations as other cognitive tasks. That is, creativity can be discussed using the same information processing concepts found throughout this chapter. For example, generating new ideas involves information retrieval from long-term memory, activation of associations, and integration and transformation of representations (e.g., propositional networks, images). Evaluation of novel ideas or artefacts involves inferring relationships, pattern matching, and hypothesis testing, among other operations. As with other cognitive tasks, working memory capacity is often a limiting factor, and as a result we engage in various simplification strategies. Unfortunately, these strategies become barriers to creative thought when, for example, we generate only one or two alternative ideas, we fail to evaluate ideas on more than a few dimensions, and we fail to reject familiar constraints for how items should look or be used. The last of these problems—our failure to think of new ways to use a very familiar concept or object—is called functional fixedness. For example, when we see a hammer, we may have difficulty moving beyond our immediate associations with the acts of pounding or prying. Yet, in the right circumstances, it might be both novel and useful to think of the hammer as a way to prop open a window or as a hanger to support wind chimes.

One problem we face when confronted with a problem that requires a creative solution is that we have trouble sustaining the “idea generation” phase of the creative process. One reason is that, from the outset, the cognitive load is high. In addition, because novel objects and ideas tend to increase arousal, it is likely that the production of novelty will create an upward spiraling of arousal. This, in turn, will gradually create cognitive tunneling, bringing idea generation to a rapid close (Cropley, 1999). One countermeasure is to find ways to reduce arousal in the immediate context of problem solving, for example by reducing the prospect of immediate, harsh evaluation by supervisors. Another alternative is to simply take breaks during the generation stage, an idea that is consistent with the incubation phenomenon.

Incubation effects on creativity are often positive. In general, people are more likely to solve a problem after taking a break rather than working on a solution without interruption (Smith, 1995). Controlled trials, however, show that this advantage is not inevitable (Nickerson, 1999) and research continues to focus on learning the conditions under which incubation provides benefits. It is possible that a break from the act of novelty generation may serve to reduce arousal to more task-appropriate levels. Another explanation is that the probability of a new problem representation being put into action (e.g., the mental image or list of procedural steps being manipulated to generate solutions) is greater when a person disrupts his or her own processing. We may simply be more likely to forget ineffective parts of prior problem representations when we return to the task. This may be one instance when an interruption is actually a good thing for cognitive performance.

The importance of the cognitive representation of problems, and the different display formats that support these representations, has been demonstrated for a variety of problem-solving tasks (Davidson & Sternberg, 1998). Flexible visualization tools may be particularly valuable for creative problem solving, because changing the orientation, color scheme, format, or level of focus will change the salience of different aspects of the problem. Product designers working on a new lamp design, for example, benefited from the use of software that allowed them to shift between multi-color and single-color views (Damle, 2010). Returning to the proximity compatibility principle (PCP, Section 4.6.2), making all the parts of the lamp the same color (increasing display proximity) allowed the designers to more easily integrate the parts of their design and focus on emergent features of the overall shape. Multi-colored lamp images, on the other hand, although more photorealistic, led designers to prematurely focus on details. The development of software tools that reduce problems like functional fixedness, that instead encourage the perception of different aspects of the problem, are an important focus of current work on the design of creativity support tools (Schneiderman, 2009).

Finally, ending quite literally on a positive note, research indicates that being in a happier mood is associated with creative thinking. Meta-analyses have revealed that active, positive affect (i.e., happiness) is related to the highest levels of creativity in a wide variety of tasks; active, negative affect (i.e., fear and anxiety) are associated with the lowest levels (Baas et al., 2008;

Davis, 2009). Explanations for the mood-creativity association have centered on the relationship between positive affect and “breadth of attention,” which in problem solving involves seeing more elements of the problem space as potentially relevant to the solution (Isen et al., 1987).

## 5.6 Metacognition

We end our discussion of higher-order cognitive processes by discussing a type of knowledge that may have a profound impact on the successful performance of any task, but especially on tasks involving problem solving, comprehension, and the maintenance of situation awareness. The term metacognition was introduced by Flavell (1979) to indicate a person’s knowledge about his or her own cognitive processes and, further, the use of this information to regulate performance (Reder, 1996; Rhodes, 2019). The most active area of research on metacognition has been in education, where researchers have looked at how students’ beliefs about their own information-processing capabilities influence learning strategies and ultimate academic success (Bjork, 1999; Veenman, van Hout-Wolters, & Afflerbach, 2006). However, the concept has important implications for the practice of human factors and ergonomics as well.

When describing metacognition, most researchers distinguish between metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive control processes. In general, metacognitive knowledge includes beliefs about one’s own processing capacity, about potential strategies that enhance performance (or minimize capacity limits), and about when and why such strategies are appropriate (Schraw & Moshman, 1995). For example, an expert operator may come to the conclusion that it is more difficult to notice critical signals when they occur in a particular region of a visual display. Further, the operator may believe that he or she can compensate by oversampling that region but may also believe that oversampling will come at the cost of much greater mental effort. At the other end of the meta-cognitive spectrum—the lack of metacognitive knowledge—Levine et al. (2000) have noted that most people are unaware of their strong tendencies toward change blindness discussed in Section 3.1.2, a metacognitive phenomenon referred to as “change blindness blindness.” Clearly, such beliefs can influence the strategies an operator chooses. It is important to realize that these beliefs may not be accurate and, further, that individuals, especially experts, may sometimes be unaware of the assumptions they are making (Chi et al., 1988; Ward et al., 2019).

Metacognitive control processes include planning, monitoring, and evaluating one’s own performance (Schraw & Moshman, 1995). We might associate many of these processes with the functions of Baddeley’s (2003) central executive in working memory discussed in Section 5.1. Planning includes determining the appropriate allocation of attention and time to different parts of a task as well as decisions about what aspects of performance to sacrifice if capacity limits create mandatory trade-offs (e.g., would a fast but inaccurate strategy be better than an accurate but slow one?). Monitoring involves keeping track of the quality of performance as a task progresses, for example, our ability to know whether or not we comprehend some written instructions well enough to act on them; or for the learner, whether we have studied enough on one lesson to have mastered the material and move on to the next (Rhodes, Cleary, & DeLoche, 2019). Finally, evaluation looks at the products of task performance and the control processes used to obtain them. This allows an assessment of how effectively we deployed our limited cognitive resources and may further elaborate our metacognitive knowledge in long-term memory.

Metacognitive knowledge and control processes are important for understanding human performance in a variety of domains. One important application is to determine how metacognitive knowledge may shape users’ preferences for and use of specific interface and product designs. Users’ preference choices may sometimes seem less than optimal based on existing performance data or predictions of formal performance models (Andre & Wickens, 1995). Cases in point are users’ “intuitive” judgments of product usability. Payne (1995; see also Vu & Proctor, 2003), for example, explored users judgments about the compatibility of different arrangements of multi-element displays and controls. These judgments were not accurate predictors of actual performance using the different display–control arrangements. In short, the participants undervalued (or, perhaps, did not understand) the importance of configural and compatibility properties on memory and performance.

Smallman and St. John (2005) propose that many users and designers alike fall prey to naïve realism, a tendency to prefer more realistic-looking displays, even when simpler formats would support better performance. In general, these authors attribute users’ preferences to faulty metacognitive knowledge. For example, most individuals seem unaware of the inherent ambiguities of size and depth found in more realistic-looking 3D displays (see Section 4.4). They were also unaware of the relatively small portion of complex displays that they could process in a single glance, and they seemed not to consider the visual search costs that could result from increased display complexity.

Other examples of the impact of both metacognitive knowledge and control processes are found in drivers’ overconfidence in their driving abilities in a variety of situations, particularly those involving multi-tasking (Horrey, Lesch, & Gabaret, 2009: see Section 7 of this chapter). For example, nighttime driving, as well as the use of devices such as cell phones, selectively degrades focal (central) vision which is critical for detecting hazards. Peripheral vision, which provides sufficient information for lane keeping, is relatively unimpaired by such factors. However, drivers may not appreciate the distinctive functions of each visual subsystem and may take satisfactory lane keeping as evidence that they have suffered no impairment from nighttime viewing conditions or in-vehicle distractions (Leibowitz et al., 1982). This leads to dangerous overconfidence in their limited ability to detect and identify hazards at night, a task using a very different visual system and resources (see Section 7.2). Hence, they drive too fast. In this case, metacognitive monitoring and performance evaluation are impaired, in part because the drivers have continuous feedback about lane keeping but only infrequent feedback about hazard detection. In addition, the driver’s inadequate knowledge about their own perceptual systems may not lead them to suspect that one visual subsystem can be spared while another is degraded.

When correctly diagnosed, metacognitive errors can be addressed in a variety of ways. Training is one approach, for example, providing information about the types of displays that best support different types of tasks (Milkman, Clugh, & Bazerman, 2009). Shen et al. (2012) found that the failure of users to select the appropriate perspective views to use when performing different emergency management tasks could be partially corrected with very simple verbal guidance about the best use of 2D versus 3D displays. Alternatively, poor strategy choices (or poor use of technology) might be addressed by providing better performance feedback to help users recalibrate their perceptions of their own skill levels, knowledge, and capabilities and to allow them to learn which performance strategies are most effective.

In Section 5, we have discussed information-processing tasks that are deliberative, time consuming, require extensive cognitive resources, and for which the “correct” response is poorly defined and multiple responses are possible, even desirable. We turn now to characteristics of actions that are typically selected rapidly, sometimes without much effort, and often without great uncertainty about their outcome.

## 6 ACTION SELECTION

Many of the sources of variability in the speed and accuracy of selecting actions, in response to an event, were covered in detail in Chapter 4 in this volume by Proctor and Vu, and will only be briefly reviewed, and sometimes augmented here.

## 6.1 Information Content and Choice Complexity

Vu and Proctor describe how the speed of selecting an action is directly proportional to the formal information content of the action choice, as quantified by information theory. Thus, the choice between the two actions (1 bit) of whether to swerve left or right in the face of a hazard object on the road is simpler, and faster, than the choice between three (braking, left or right). And if a fourth option is added: continue and run over the hazard, the choice between these four actions (2 bits) is slower still. Using the language of information theory, this choice time can be pre-cisely predicted by the Hick-Hyman Law (Hick, 1952; Hyman, 1953). Each added bit of the choice uncertainty, from 1 bit (2 choices) to 2 bits (4 choices), to 3 bits (8 choices) produces a proportionately greater time to process (and therefore respond to) the stimulus event.

An extension of the Hick-Hyman Law can be applied to expectancy. Low probability (and therefore high information content) events that are therefore unexpected, are responded to more slowly, with a slowing that can be quantitatively predicted by the Hick-Hyman Law. At one extreme, events that are totally expected (p=1.0) like the sun rising, convey 0 bits of information. At the other extreme, so-called “black swan” events, such as the 9/11 attack on the World Trade Center have an extremely high information content.

## 6.2 Compatibility

As described in Chapter 4 in considerable detail, response time is heavily influenced by the compatibility of the mapping from stimulus to response, as illustrated by the simple case that it takes longer to press a left button in response to a light appearing on the right side of a screen, than to respond with a left press to a light on the left side of a display panel. It also takes longer to say “right” to the left-appearing light than it does to say “left” to the same light. Several different manifestations of stimulus-response, or event-action compatibility are described by Proctor and Vu in Chapter 4.

## 6.3 Sequential Effects

Proctor and Vu describe how response time to a particular stimulus is influenced by the sequence of stimulus-response events that appeared on prior trials. Repeated actions, to the same repeated stimulus are more rapid than are responses to a change in stimulus from the previous one, a benefit called the repetition effect. However, we note here that that with very rapidly repeated actions, such as the keyboard letter presses when transcribing text, alternations tend to be more rapid than repetitions because of the need to reactivate the same muscle group in repetitions as, for example, when typing zzzzzzzzz (Sternberg, Kroll, & Wright, 1978).

## 6.4 Serial Response Time

The rapid responses of typing, or the rapid stimulus-response RTs when transcribing, whether transcribing printed musical notes to piano keys, or words spoken to a UN language translator, bring to bear many of the same issues of the single S-R response above, but also adds some new issues. When the task requires several sequential RTs, it is referred to as serial RT (Wickens, Helton, et al., 2022). We address three important issues in serial RT below.

## 6.4.1 Parallel Processing

First, transcribing can be extremely rapid. The minimum choice RT for a single one bit 2-choice mapping is over 200 msec. Yet a skilled typist can execute up over 10 key presses per second, an RT of less than 100 msec, when selecting among 26 possible responses. How is this possible? Proctor and Vu point to the key role of preparation and advanced information, or preview, in supporting faster RT. The typist, transcribing written text, can look ahead and then hold the perceived letters in a buffer memory until they are typed (Shaffer, 1973), such that the typist will be looking at a word a few words ahead of those his fingers are typing. In addition, familiarity with the text material allows chunking of letters such that, for example, “the” is perceived as a single unit (see Section 5.1), held as a single chunk, and responded to as a group or motor program of 3 key responses, the motor program also addressed by Proctor and Vu. This chunking and parallel processing between perception, memory and response allows the transcription to proceed quite efficiently.

## 6.4.2 Decision Complexity Advantage

The second issue that serial RT raises is the tradeoff in total information transmission efficiency between stimulus frequency and S-R mapping complexity. Can a person transmit more total information (bits/second) with a greater number of simple choices (e.g., 1 bit, as in Morse code), or a smaller number of more complex choices (e.g., 3+ bits as in typing)? Equivalence of transmission rates between these two cases would suggest that the maximum speed of Morse code responses is about three times that of typing. But in fact, typing from a 26-letter keyboard is much more efficient (bits/second) than Morse coding.

This difference reflects a much more general principle of information processing: the decision complexity advantage (Wickens, Hilton et al., 2021). People make more efficient information processors with a smaller number of complex decisions than a larger number of simple ones. It explains, in part, how information option choice is more rapid with a single 8-item menu (3 bits) than keying through three embedded 2-item menus (3X1 bit). Wickens, Hollands, et al. (2013) provide several other examples of the decision complexity advantage, including chording keyboards and “macro keys” where a single keypress can create a single common word like “the.”

## 6.4.3 Pacing

A third issue that serial RT raises is related to pacing. If the user is able to control the speed with which stimulus events arrive, as in transcription typing, this is called self-pacing. In contrast, if stimulus arrival rate is controlled by another agent, such as the speaker’s words to a UN language translator, or to the sign language interpreter for the hearing-impaired, this is called forced pacing. Sometimes the choice of schedules can be made by the workplace designer. Traditional assembly lines of parts on a conveyer belt dictate a forced paced schedule. But an inspector on a single screen computer can run on a self-paced schedule, taking as long as needed to process each stimulus event (image) to a classification response before requesting the next screen image.

Given such an important distinction between schedules, the question arises “which is better?” It turns out that the answer is not simple (Wickens, Hilton et al., 2021), but one key factor is the extent to which the human processing time is variable between stimuli (e.g., in image inspection, image quality varies a lot between images). Greater variability favors the self-paced schedule.

## 6.5 Response Confusability

Whenever a set of manual responses are specified, any increases in the similarity between them (decreases in discriminability) will increase the likelihood of confusion. Thus, movement of the control stick to either one of two forward positions is a response choice that has greater opportunity for confusion than movement in either a forward or backward direction. Correspondingly, two buttons that look alike are more confusable (and hence error prone) than are two that are differently colored or shape-coded. Although making controls physically distinct from each other may sometimes destroy a sense of aesthetics in design, such distinctions will generally lead to improved human reliability (Norman, 1988). Incidentally, increased similarity between voice control options will also produce the same increase in error likelihood, although here the mediating agent is the voice recognition agent (whether human or computer) rather than the human responder. Thus, the vocabulary selected for use in a voice control application should be chosen with a mind to avoiding confusable-sounding articulations, such as “to” and “through.”

## 6.6 The Speed-Accuracy Tradeoff

A final issue relevant to both single and serial RT, addressed by Proctor and Vu in Chapter 4 is the speed-accuracy tradeoff (Drury, 1994; Fitts, 1966), transcending almost all aspects and stages of human-information processing. Trying (or being forced) to respond rapidly produces errors, while trying to be accurate slows down performance. Slower performance yields fewer decisions per second, but more rapid performance can yield less information transmitted (more errors) per decision. We can see how these two factors trade off as the stress for speed versus accuracy is varied (Drury, 1994). It turns out that optimal performance is produced at the midrange of this trade-off (Howell & Kreidler, 1964), which is a level that people tend to, optimally, seek. This is because, at one extreme, excessive speed stress will produce chance accuracy (0 bits/second), but at the other extreme, excessive stress for accuracy (e.g., a goal that might be set by management of a company to achieve zero errors) tends to produce unacceptably long response times and hence can slow production to a near halt (Wickens, Hilton et al., 2021).

The implications of the speed accuracy tradeoff or “SATO” in industry are manifold and four are highlighted here:

1. For single responses, such as the response to an unexpected systems failure, workers should be cautioned against making excessively rapid responses, in spite of the fact that instinct may predispose them to extreme speed. In most cases it is important to take necessary time to understand the situation before taking vital actions.

2. In many safety-critical systems and activities, the SATO defines the tradeoff between safety (accuracy, avoiding errors) and productivity (speed). Management, or users themselves, should clearly understand how instructions or environmental context can influence the safety-productivity SATO, sometimes to unacceptable levels in sacrificing safety.

3. As described in the previous section, management decisions to impose a forced-paced schedule in serial RT have important SATO implications, depending on the established event rate (e.g., conveyer belt speed).

4. In some circumstances, we can observe a speed-accuracy trade-on, such that slower responses lead to reduced, rather than increased accuracy. In particular, for any task requiring some use of working memory between stimulus event and response, accuracy may suffer with a more delayed response, as the quality of working memory for the stimulus information may degrade before a response is given (Wickens, Hilton et. al., 2021).

## 6.7 Continuous Manual Control

A long sequence of visual stimuli and spatially guided manual responses in serial RT offers a transition from discrete transcription to continuous manual control or tracking (Jagacinski & Flach, 2003). The single S-R version of this task is covered by Vu and Proctor in their discussion of Fitts’s Law in Chapter 4. Here we discuss the continuous (tracking) version: a series of control “wiggles” the human makes in response to a time-varying visual signals. Any tracking task, like driving a car, riding a bike, flying a plane or threading an endoscopic probe down a vessel can be represented by the tracking loop as in Figure 13.

In Figure 13, an error between desired position or velocity (the target) and the current position or velocity (the cursor, or controlled vehicle) is a time-varying function e(t) that is perceived on a display by the human operator. A response is then executed to the control device (e.g., the steering wheel, yoke of the plane, the handlebars of the bike, or flow control in an industrial process) and the dynamics of the controlled system translates that manual response into a changing system position and trajectory (the output, o(t)) relative to the ideal target state. The intent of the control response by the operator is to make the difference between desired and observed state—the error—equal to 0. As the feedback loop in Figure 13 indicates, this is called “closed loop tracking” with a negative feedback loop, in which the control is exercised in a direction opposite to the error. (If your car is veering to the right of the lane-center, you turn the steering wheel to the left.) Hence the negation, or subtraction.

As with discrete reaction time tasks, so with tracking, a number of factors influence the difficulty, and so will produce greater error, when this error is averaged over the duration of the tracking task period. Specifically tracking difficulty, and therefore both error and mental workload is increased by an increase in:

1. The bandwidth, which is essentially the frequency of “wiggles” in the displayed error and therefore the frequency with which compensatory corrections are needed. This is analogous to the event rate of a forced pace schedule in discrete information transcription tasks described in the previous section. Higher bandwidth results from three sources: (a) higher bandwidth of the command input in Figure 13 (e.g., a more curving “wiggling” road, or a faster driving speed on a curvy road); higher bandwidth of a disturbance, which itself can come (b) from more turbulence in the environment, or (c) from the tracker’s own control output that is unrelated to the input (e.g., jittering the control, or other erroneous control movement caused, for example, by a sneeze). A bandwidth of a random, unpredictable input greater than about 1 Hz makes manual tracking nearly impossible (Wickens, 1986).

2. The lag between when a control is exercised and when the system responds.

A transmission lag is a fixed delay such as when controlling a lunar vehicle from the Earth. Here it takes a full 7 seconds between when a control is exercised and its effect is seen on the Earth-located display. The transmission lag makes tracking a high bandwidth input extremely difficult. Even lags of less than half a second can be detrimental to some closed loop tracking tasks, such as those in flight simulators.

• A control dynamics lag is determined by the calculus derivative of how the system responds to a step change in the position of the control. As shown in Figure 14:

A zero-order system or position dynamics responds with a change in position on the display. This is similar to how the screen-displayed cursor responds to the change of position of a mouse, or of the finger on a finger pad.

A first-order system or velocity dynamics responds with a change in velocity of the vehicle or other controlled element. A car’s heading is a first-order response to the steering wheel position since a given deflection angle of the wheel to a new position will cause a proportional change in turn rate (defined by the curvature or radius of the turn).

A second-order system or acceleration dynamics responds with an acceleration to a given change in position of the control input. This would be the car’s lateral position in the lane. If the steering wheel is deflected a fixed angle off center, the fixed position (and therefore error)

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 13 The tracking loop.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 14 Increased lag with increasing control order.

initially deviate slowly, but then more rapidly as the car starts to turn more sharply. Another example of a second-order system is the initial acceleration of any heavy sluggish vehicle to a fixed increase in power, like a rocket, aircraft or ship, responding to an increase in thrust. The change is initially slow, but then progressively more rapid such that position along track follows an accelerating curve.

Thus, the order of system dynamics corresponds to the calculus derivative of the position. As shown in Figure 14, generally, higher- order systems produce greater lags, and hence, like transmission lags, cause increased tracking difficulty and mental workload (Wickens, 1986). In Figure 14, the step change in control input to the system is at the top. The over-time response of the system is shown in the three functions below.

The characteristics of dynamic responses go well beyond physical systems whose response is defined by the Newtonian motion and thermodynamic laws, and extend to biological and even financial and cultural systems. The recent example of the coronavirus pandemic spread provides a tragic example. The response of infection prevalence follows an accelerating second-order response to the input (the abrupt introduction of infected people into a population), so there is a lag of approximately 7–10 days. And the lag from infection introduction to the change in fatality rate is even longer. People’s failure to appreciate this lag, and respond appropriately early enough, has resulted in unnecessary fatalities.

In order to effectively “track” (i.e., respond in a desired error-correcting direction to) the output of a lagged system, it is necessary to predict what that error will be in the future, and not what it is in the current state. If responding only to the current state of a system with lags, by the time the corrective response is realized, after the lag, by a change in system state, it will be too late. This brings us to the third element that makes tracking hard:

3. Lack of prediction. The lack of prediction can be restated in the opposite (more positive) terms, as the presence of predictive, future information about the state of a lagged system and such prediction will almost always make tracking easier. Prediction itself can come from two sources:

Skill and the mental model. Skilled trackers will learn that the optimal prediction of the future state of a lagged system is the rate of change or first derivative of the present state. Thus, if we pay attention to the rate of deviation of the car from the lane center, and not just how close we are to the center of the lane, and respond with control in the opposite direction proportionate to that rate, we will be more effective in control. And responding proportionally to the acceleration of the error signal (e.g., the rate of change of turn rate), while harder, is even more effective. We describe this control strategy as possessing a more accurate “mental model” of the systems dynamics, accuracy that is gained by system experience and training.

Predictive displays. It is also possible to design a display system that explicitly infers the future position or velocity of error, both by using automation models of the dynamics to calculate the predicted change in system response seconds, minutes (or even days, in the case of a pandemic) and by inferring the predicted state of the environment. Such predictions can then be explicitly displayed, as the basis for more effective control. In the language of situation awareness (see Section 5.4, Endsley, Chapter 17 in this volume), this is directly supporting level 3 SA. These displays have been extremely valuable in controlling sluggish systems like larger aircraft (Wickens, Gempler, & Morphew, 2000), ships (van Breda, 1999), and industrial process control variables (whose thermodynamic response to inputs, like applied heat, may also be sluggish and lagged; Yin, Wickens Helander, & LaBerge, 2015).

Many dynamic systems for which manual tracking was once required are now equipped with automatic control, as discussed in Chapter 55 on aerospace by Landry, and Chapter 52, on automation by Sawyer et al. But many are not and can still benefit from predictive displays; and even with those that are, the human supervisor may need to intervene and jump back into the loop, should the auto-control unexpectedly fail. Predictive displays will make that re-entry far more fluent.

## 6.8 Errors

The previous discussion has focused primarily on the time required to process and respond to various items of information. Yet in many systems the occurrence of errors is more critical than the occurrence of delays in processing. That is, the loss of information, rather than its transmission delay, is the factor of greatest concern. Although errors are treated extensively in Chapter 20 of this volume by Liu et al., we wish here to highlight the manner in which different classes of errors can be categorized in the context of the flow of information as depicted in Figure 2 (Norman, 1981; Reason, 1990, 1997, 2008).

First, mistakes represent errors of the earlier stages of information processing, in which incorrect action is carried out as a result of a failure to understand the nature of a situation (i.e., a failure of stage 2 or stage 3 situation awareness, as discussed in Section 5.2). This may result from a breakdown in perception or working memory or from insufficient knowledge to interpret the available cues (i.e., knowledge-based errors). Second, while a situation may be diagnosed and understood correctly, rule-based errors may result from a failure to apply the correct rules appropriately for selection of a response (Reason, 1990). Third, errors may result from slips of action, when the correct response is intended but an incorrect action is actually released (i.e., an unintended response “slips” out of the hands or mouth) (Norman, 1981). Slips of this sort are typically the result of poor human factors design, such as incompatible control–display relationships (see Section 6.5), confusable displays (Section 1) or controls (Section 6.7), coupled with an operator who is well skilled and performing a task in a highly automated mode, thereby not carefully monitoring his or her own action selections.

A particular version of the slip is called the mode error, often observed in multi-modal systems, where the operator forgets that the system is in one mode, thinking it is in another one, and executes a series of actions which have a very different effect on the system than intended. A trivial case is when a typist, without using visual feedback, is unaware that the keyboard is in the caps mode. In safety-critical systems, however, mode errors can have major consequences, as, for example, when a speed control can be set to a digital value which controls kilometers per hour or meters per second, depending on the mode setting. Clearly, such multi-mode systems must be accompanied by salient feedback of the current mode.

Errors can also be attributed directly to a breakdown of memory. As noted in Section 5.1, memory breakdowns may lead to forgetting or confusion of material, whereas errors of prospective memory may lead operators to forget to perform some action that was previously intended (Loukopopolous, Dismukes, & Barshi, 2009). Often described as errors of omission, these are typified by leaving the last copied paper on the glass of a photocopier or failing to tighten the bolts after completing a maintenance task (Reason, 1997).

It is usually the case that the conditions that are associated with slower processing are those that also produce more errors, and hence design remediation based on measures of processing speed will be productive in improving overall system accuracy. However, in certain circumstances, a strategic adjustment in how an operator performs a task will lead to an inverse relationship between speed and accuracy: the speed–accuracy trade-off discussed above. In this case, a “set” to respond rapidly will lead to more rather than fewer errors (Drury, 1994). An example here would be that of the effects of time stress in emergencies, which may lead to hasty but error-prone actions in the processing of information.

## 7 MULTI-TASKING

People are often challenged at multi-tasking, a conclusion well validated with automobile accident statistics (Caird et al., 2018;

Regan, Lee, & Young, 2009), in the classroom (Kirshner & de Bruyckere 2017) as well as being documented by the frequency of interruptions in the workplace (Gonzales & Mark, 2004) and in the hospital (Sanderson, McCurdie & Grungeiger, 2019). The study of multi-tasking is itself a subdiscipline of the study of attention (Johnson & Proctor, 2004; Wickens, 2021; Wickens & McCarley, 2008), where the focus is on the strengths and weaknesses in dividing attention between tasks (Salvucci & Taatgen, 2011; Wickens, 2013).

Understanding the nature and causes of these challenges in multi-tasking requires consideration of two quite different modes of multi-tasking: sequential, in which tasks are performed one at a time such as the alternation between head-down texting and head-up driving in a vehicle, and concurrent, when two activities are carried out more or less in parallel such as driving while listening to the radio, or walking while talking. We treat these two modes separately in the following sections.

## 7.1 Sequential Multi-Tasking

Three different research paradigms address the factors that affect the fluency and efficiency of sequential multi-tasking.

## 7.1.1 Interruption Management

Interruption management applies to a situation, shown schematically in Figure 15, in which a person is carrying out an ongoing task (OT), like driving a car, monitoring a patient, or carrying out an aviation checklist, and is unexpectedly interrupted by a discrete interrupting task (IT) like a phone call or an arriving text message. Attention is switched, at S1, from the OT to the IT, and full attention is then focused on the IT until it is either completed, or the person decides to switch back to the OT (S2 in Figure 15). A large amount of research, much of it in the domain of human-computer interaction (Jacko, 2012) has examined properties of the task and workstation that can affect the fluency and optimality of interruption management at both S1 and S2 (e.g., Katioditis &Taatgen, 2014; Salvucci & Taatgen, 2011; Trafton & Monk, 2007).

Key factors include:

At S1

The greater engagement in the OT that might delay the switch to the IT (Horrey, Lesch, Gabaret, Simmoons, & Rammohan, 2017; Iani & Wickens, 2007; Wickens, Gutzwiller, & Santamaria, 2015).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 15 The anatomy of an interruption.

The greater salience of the arrival of the IT, a factor discussed in the context of attention capture in Section 3.1.2. The phone call is typically more salient than the arrival of the text message; and both of these auditory events are more salient than the silent arrival of an e-mail. Greater IT salience will shorten S1.

• The cognitive strategy adopted by the person to delay the switch at S1 either:

Until a “stopping point” in the OT is reached (e.g., “wait until I finish the paragraph”). Trafton and colleagues refer to this as a “subgoal completion” (Altmann & Trafton, 2002; Trafton & Monk, 2007).

Until you take the time to rehearse where you are in the OT, or put a physical placeholder on the OT (e.g., a pencil mark or yellow sticky note on the item just completed on a checklist; McDaniel et al., 2004).

Both of the above have been well validated to improve the fluency of return at S2, particularly in aviation, where fluent interruption management is vital for safety (e.g., Loukoupoulis, Dismukes & Barshi, 2009).

## During the IT

The subsequent return to the OT at S2 is hindered by longer and more difficult ITs, which, by diverting cognitive resources away from the memory of what you were doing on the OT, makes return more challenging. However, this return at S2 is assisted when some representation of the OT remains visible in the person’s field of view (Ratwani, Trafton, & Boehm-Davis, 2010).

## At S2

The “interruption lag” is the time it takes to accomplish S2, and the more general term “fluency of return.” includes both the interruption lag, and also the extent to which the OT is picked up where it was left off, without error. If the OT is a checklist task, this can be of vital importance if the checklist is resumed after missing (and therefore skipping) a critical item upon return (Loukoupolis et al., 2009). The most important variables influencing the fluency of the return are, as described above, the rehearsal and placeholding strategies carried out at S1, along with the increased OT visibility and the reduced time and resource demand of the IT.

In addition to these factors, computer interventions can be imposed to improve interruption management, such as salient reminders to return to the OT or automatic “placeholders” implemented via, for example, a blinking light on the most recent item accomplished in a checklist. In human–computer interaction it has also been argued that an intelligent interruption management software can sense, from the operator’s keypress activity, when a subgoal has been completed, and defer delivery of the IT (e.g., an arriving text message) until that time (Bailey & Konstan, 2006). For example, mobile phones could be designed to defer the “ring” until a car is stopped (Reagan &Cicchino, 2020).

## 7.1.2 Task-Switching Alternation

Much of the basic laboratory research on task switching, reviewed in Chapter 4, is based on a paradigm initially introduced by Jersild (1927) and subsequently expanded by Monsell (2003) and many other researchers. Here the participant sees a series of stimuli, for example, digits or letters and needs to classify these (e.g., if digits, as high or low, or odd or even, or if letters, as consonants or vowels). The participant will sometimes apply the same classification rule for a series of trials and then be required to switch the task classification rule, i.e., from odd-even digits to high-low digits. Through a wide number of variations on this paradigm, researchers have established several factors that affect this task switching fluency, reviewed in Chapter 4 by Proctor and Vu, with a key conclusion that the act of switching is itself cognitively demanding. But the paradigm lacks the ecological validity of a large body of real world task switching, in which the decision to switch tasks is voluntary, there may be more than two tasks to switch between, and the tasks may be quite heterogeneous in nature (e.g., the switch between driving and phone operations; Janssen, Brumby, & Rae, 2012).

## 7.1.3 Voluntary Task Switching/Task Management

In the voluntary task switching paradigm people are assigned two or more tasks to perform, all of which are time-consuming, like completing a schedule planning task and filling out a time-sheet (a two-task version, Gilbert & Wickens, 2017) or, as a more complex example, an astronaut in emergency switching between failure diagnosis, following safety steps, communications with ground control and navigation (a four-task version); or an emergency room doctor (Barg-Walkow et al., 2020). One may think of these and other example as a series of OT-IT sequences, except that once a switch is made, the chosen task now becomes the OT, and all other tasks become “Alternative tasks” (ATs) “clamoring for attention.” At issue is how people schedule and manage the multi-task ensemble confronting them.

Wickens, Gutzwiller, and Santamaria (2015) carried out a meta-analysis of studies of voluntary task switching and interruption management and identified four factors that had a substantial effect the likelihood that an AT task would be switched “to” in a multi-task ensemble, and or would resist being switched away “from,” once it became an OT. These four factors of voluntary task switching, bearing some analogy to the four parameters of the SEEV model of visual attention switching discussed in Section 3, are:

Task salience, as defined in interruption management (Section 7.1.1). Here auditory tasks, or those signaling their arrival with a sound, and tactile tasks, are both more salient than visual (Lu 2013; Sarter et al., 2013). And within each modality, greater intensity is more salient. Important also are tasks with 0 salience. These are tasks which require the performer to use prospective memory to remember to return to them (Dismukes & Nowinski, 2007; Loukopolis et al., 2009), and these tasks are particularly vulnerable to neglect.

Task priority establishes, where possible, the doctrinal or imposed value of performing each task in the ensemble. In aviation, it is clearly established through training that keeping the plane aloft (avoiding stalling) has a higher priority than navigating, which has higher priority than communicating (see Landry, Chapter 55 in this volume). In driving, hazard avoidance has a higher priority than navigating.

Task interest is a variable that is personal and will differ from person to person for a given task (Gilbert & Wickens, 2017; Wickens, Gutzwiller et al., 2016,). However, a task rated as higher interest by a certain person will both attract attention to be switched to, and once initiated will be more resistant to being switched away from.

All three of the above task attributes are uniform attractors to an attention switch when they are ATs, and sustainers when they are properties of the OT. However, the fourth variable: task difficulty exerts a more complex effect. As an AT, more difficult tasks are less attractive and will be avoided. But once engaged as an OT, the more difficult task now often has an attracting attribute, in which it is more likely to be sustained.

Together, all four parameters above, coupled with an inherent switch resistance (a tendency to stay on whatever task one is performing) as a means of effort conservation, have been combined in a model to predict switching between heterogeneous tasks, called the STOM model (strategic task overload management; Wickens, Gutzwiller et al., 2015, 2016). This model, a close cousin of models based on queuing theory (Liu, 2013; Wu & Liu in Chapter 26 in this volume), can be considered a form of optimality model, to predict the extent to which a person’s actual multi-tasking strategy adheres to a strategy deemed optimal (e.g., switching driven primarily by priority). Another important feature of the STOM model, is that, by predicting consecutive durations of time (model update cycles) on which attention stays on any task in an ensemble, the model can equally well predict successive periods of time during which attention stays away from a given task; that is, periods of task neglect or cognitive tunneling (St Lot, Imbert, & Dehaise, 2020; Wickens & Alexander, 2009). Cognitive tunneling is closely related to the issue of visual tunneling or “fixation” discussed in Section 3, and the two are more or less synonymous when applied to a set of exclusively visual tasks. However cognitive tunneling also addresses attention to (or neglect of) tasks that may be auditory or purely cognitive in nature, such as planning, mind wandering or maintaining situation awareness.

Collectively, results from studies of interruption management, task switching, and task management have allowed researchers to piece together a fairly coherent picture of how people behave when the demands of tasks are sufficiently high that two tasks simply cannot be performed at the same time; such may characterize periods in which total task demand or workload is “over the red line” (see Hancock et al., Chapter 7 in this volume); but short of this, people will often carry out tasks concurrently (although not always perfectly), and in Section 7.2 we address the task and individual characteristics that modulate their ability to do so successfully.

## 7.2 Concurrent Processing

In contrast to sequential processing, an understanding of concurrent processing, whether perfect parallel processing or degraded processing showing a dual task decrement, depends on somewhat different mechanisms. These mechanisms are as closely related to the structure of the information-processing sequences within the tasks themselves as they are to the operator’s knowledge of task importance and priority (although there are interactions between these two influences; Gopher, 1992). Here human factors interest is in the task features that can enable any sort of concurrent processing to emerge from serial processing and that can enable that concurrent processing to avoid substantial dual task decrements. Four characteristics appear to influence this degree of success: (1) task similarity; (2) task demand; (3) task resource structure; and (4) allocation policy (Wickens, 2002, 2008; Wickens, Helton, et al., 2022), although how these influences are exerted is somewhat complex.

## 7.2.1 Task Similarity

A high degree of similarity between two tasks may induce confusion between their elements, just as similarity between perceptual signals will cause confusion (Section 3.3), high similarity between items held in working memory will increase the degree of interference between them (Section 5.1), or high similarity between two response devices will increase the possibility of confusion of actions (Section 6.5). In the context of interruption management discussed above, high similarity between the OT and the IT will degrade performance, because the remembered status of the OT will get confused with material from the IT (Cellier & Eyrolle, 1992; Dismukes & Nowinski, 2007). An example of high similarity in concurrent task performance would be adding test scores in grading exams, while listening to sports scores or a stock market report.

In contrast to similarity of material, when the rules governing two tasks are more similar this may actually allow the tasks to be better integrated, fostering more effective concurrent processing. This may involve using similar control dynamics on two axes of a tracking task (Chernikoff & LeMay, 1963; Fracker & Wickens, 1989) or using similar rules to map stimuli (events) to responses (actions) (Duncan, 1979).

## 7.2.2 Task Demand

Two easier tasks are better able to be performed concurrently (and perfectly) than are two more difficult or demanding tasks, an intuitive effect well documented in the study of cell phone interference with driving (Collet et al., 2010). We argue that easier tasks are generally more automated and consume less mental effort or resources than do more difficult ones. They impose less mental workload (see Hancock et al., Chapter 7 in this volume). Such automaticity can often be achieved by extensive practice on what are called consistently mapped tasks (Fisk et al., 1987). These are tasks in which in each encounter by the learner, certain properties of the relation between the displayed elements, cognitive operations, and responses remain constant. Such consistent mapping will lead not only to more rapid performance but also to performance that is relatively attention-free and hence will allow other tasks to be time-shared successfully.

## 7.2.3 Task Resource Structure

Certain structural differences between two time-shared tasks increase the efficiency of their concurrent processing, as if the two tasks demand entirely (or partially) separated mental resources within the human processing system, such that it is easier to distribute tasks across multiple resources than to focus them within a single resource (Salvucci & Taatgen, 2011; Wickens, 2002; 2008; 2000; Wickens et al., 2003). These resources appear to be defined by processing code (verbal or linguistic versus spatial), processing stage (perceptual–cognitive operations versus response operations), perceptual modality (auditory versus visual versus tactile), and visual subsystems (focal vision, required for object recognition, versus ambient vision, required for orientation and locomotion; Previc, 1998).

To briefly illustrate these dichotomies of resources, it is because of the separate spatial and verbal code resources that spatially guided manual responses may be more effectively time-shared than vocal responses when operators must concurrently rehearse verbal material; but vocal responses will be more effective than spatially guided manual ones when the operator must concurrently perform another spatial task, such as tracking (e.g., the disruption of driving caused by the spatial keypresses of cell phone dialing, Collet et al., 2010). As another example of code interference, we saw in Section 5.4 that the spatial cognitive processes involved in navigation and vehicle control are better time-shared with the verbal representation of a memorized verbal route list than with the spatial representation of a memorized map.

It is because of the separate stage-defined resources that we are often able effectively to time-share responding operations (e.g., talking) with perceptual ones (e.g., scanning). It is because of the separate perceptual resources that designers have chosen to offload the heavy visual processing load of vehicle drivers or pilots with some information presented on auditory channels (Wickens et al., 2003). Finally, it is because of the separate visual channels that we can effectively keep a car centered in the lane (using ambient vision) while searching for and reading road signs (a task requiring focal vision).

## 7.2.4 Resource Allocation

Multiple resource demand (the converse of automaticity) and resource type can predict the total amount of interference between two tasks (Wickens, 2005), but the two constructs together say nothing about the extent to which one task or the other task suffers the greater decrement or bears the brunt of that interference. This relative decrement is predicted by the resource allocation policy between the two, the third element of multiple resource model (Gopher, 2007; Wickens, 2007). Such policy will be at least partially influenced by task importance or priority, as when an experimenter designates a primary and secondary task to the participant; or the flight instructor reminds the student that aviating (avoiding a stall) has a higher priority than navigating. However other factors may come into play here, such as the difficulty of the task (greater emphasis is given to the harder task) or the task’s intrinsic interest or engagement properties, the latter describing the occasional interference of cell phone conversation with safe driving, despite the driving task’s generally greater importance.

The analogy with the parameters of the STOM model of sequential task management is evident here. The distinction is that here resource allocation is accomplished between two concurrently performed tasks and is reflected in the level of performance of each relative to its single task baseline; whereas the measures in STOM are of the likelihood that a given task will be performed at all.

The two variables of resource demand and resource structure have been integrated in a computational model of concurrent task interference, described in more detail in Wickens (2005, 2008, 2013).

## 8 CONCLUSION

In conclusion, the systems with which people must interact vary vastly in their complexity, from the simple graph or tool to things like nuclear reactors or the physiology of a patient under anesthesia. As a consequence, they vary drastically in terms of the type and degree of demands imposed on the varying information-processing components we have discussed in this chapter. In some cases, systems will impose demands on components that are quite vulnerable: working memory, predictive capabilities, and divided attention, for example. At other times they may impose on human capabilities that are a source of great strength, particularly if these sources rely on the vast store of information that we retain in long-term memory, information that assists us in pattern recognition, top-down processing, chunking, and developing plans and scripts on the basis of past experience. The importance of practice and training in the development of this knowledge base cannot be overestimated.

In addition to facilitating the performance of experts in many ways, long-term memory has a second implication for the practice of human factors. This is that predictions of human performance in many systems can be based only partially on an understanding of the generic information-processing components described in this chapter. An equal and sometimes greater partner in this prediction is extensive domain knowledge regarding the particular system with which the human is interacting. As several of the chapters in this handbook address, the best prediction of human performance must be based on the intricate interaction between the information-processing components discussed here, the domain knowledge employed by the human operator, and the physical environment within and tools with which the operator works. The reader will find all of these issues covered from multiple perspectives in other chapters of the handbook.
